full_text: Survival in patients with a high prevalence of human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer: real-world data from a national referral public hospital in South America Abstract Background: The incidence of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is rising globally. Data from South America are limited. An epidemiological shift towards a higher prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated OPSCC has been described. This study evaluates oncological outcomes in patients with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC treated with radiotherapy at a cancer referral centre in South America. Materials and methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the National Cancer Institute of Chile, including patients with non-metastatic disease treated with curative intent between 2012 and 2023. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise the data. Univariate and multivariate analyses (MVA) were conducted with logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan–Meier method. Results: A total of 146 patients were analysed; 75.3% were male, with a mean age of 60.7 years. HPV positivity (p16+) was detected in 62.3%. All patients underwent radiotherapy, with 82.8% receiving concurrent chemoradiotherapy. The 5-year overall survival was 60.9% [95% confidence interval (CI): 52.7–70.3]. p16+ [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.19–0.68; p < 0.01] was independently associated with improved survival, whereas a smoking history of ≥ 10 pack-years (HR = 2.18; p = 0.02) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 2–4 (HR = 3.30; p < 0.01) were linked to worse outcomes. Conclusions: Survival outcomes in this South American population, with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC, were comparable to internationally published data. In exploratory analyses, HPV association and concurrent chemotherapy were associated with better survival outcomes, with no significant differences between cisplatin schedules. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate survival outcomes in patients with human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer, as the incidence of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is rising globally.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the National Cancer Institute of Chile, including patients with non-metastatic disease treated with curative intent between 2012 and 2023. A total of 146 patients were analysed; 75.3% were male, with a mean age of 60.7 years.
analysis.methods: Univariate and multivariate analyses (MVA) were conducted with logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression. HPV positivity (p16+) was detected in 62.3% of patients.
analysis.main_results: The 5-year overall survival was 60.9% [95% confidence interval (CI): 52.7–70.3]. p16+ [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.19–0.68; p < 0.01] was independently associated with improved survival, whereas a smoking history of ≥ 10 pack-years (HR = 2.18; p = 0.02) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 2–4 (HR = 3.30; p < 0.01) were linked to worse outcomes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that survival outcomes in this South American population, with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC, were comparable to internationally published data. In exploratory analyses, HPV association and concurrent chemotherapy were associated with better survival outcomes, with no significant differences between cisplatin schedules.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform clinical practice and treatment strategies for HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, particularly regarding the role of concurrent chemotherapy and the impact of patient characteristics on survival outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias. The evidence is moderate as it is based on observational data rather than randomized trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated survival outcomes in patients with human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer treated at the National Cancer Institute of Chile between 2012 and 2023. A total of 146 patients were included, with 62.3% testing positive for HPV (p16+). The 5-year overall survival rate was 60.9% [95% CI: 52.7–70.3]. p16+ was independently associated with improved survival, while smoking history and ECOG performance status were linked to worse outcomes. The authors concluded that survival outcomes in this South American population were comparable to international data. The study is a retrospective cohort study, which limits the strength of the evidence to moderate.

elements_en.methods: Univariate and multivariate analyses (MVA) were conducted with logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression. HPV positivity (p16+) was detected in 62.3% of patients.
elements_en.main_results: The 5-year overall survival was 60.9% [95% confidence interval (CI): 52.7–70.3]. p16+ [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.19–0.68; p < 0.01] was independently associated with improved survival, whereas a smoking history of ≥ 10 pack-years (HR = 2.18; p = 0.02) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 2–4 (HR = 3.30; p < 0.01) were linked to worse outcomes.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that survival outcomes in this South American population, with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC, were comparable to internationally published data. elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform clinical practice and treatment strategies for HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, particularly regarding the role of concurrent chemotherapy and the impact of patient characteristics on survival outcomes.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias. The evidence is moderate as it is based on observational data rather than randomized trials.

media_mentions.content: Log In Content Articles by Type Online first Regular Issues Special collections Author Centre Guide for Authors SUBMIT News About More Advanced search About the Journal Reports of Practical Oncology and Radiotherapy Online first Survival in patients with a high prevalence of human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer: real-world data ... Online first Research paper Published online: 2026-11-13 open access View PDF Download PDF file Supp./Additional Files Supplementary files_115415 245KB Page views 35 Article views/downloads 3 Get Citation BIB ENW RIS AMA APA Chicago Harvard IEEE MLA Vancouver Connect on Social Media Facebook X LinkedIn Share E-mail alerts Receive new issue alerts (e-TOC) Sign up Survival in patients with a high prevalence of human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer: real-world data from a national referral public hospital in South America Felipe Carvajal123, Eduardo Villa4, Felipe Cardemil56, Maribel Bruna7, Felipe Bustos89, Sebastián Castro1011, Mario Tapia12, Piero Bettoli13, Fernanda Soto14, Irma Leal15, Tamara Barría161718, Héctor Contreras19 DOI: 10.5603/rpor.115415 Abstract Background: The incidence of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is rising globally. Data from South America are limited. An epidemiological shift towards a higher prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated OPSCC has been described. This study evaluates oncological outcomes in patients with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC treated with radiotherapy at a cancer referral centre in South America. Materials and methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the National Cancer Institute of Chile, including patients with non-metastatic disease treated with curative intent between 2012 and 2023. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise the data. Univariate and multivariate analyses (MVA) were conducted with logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards regression. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan–Meier method. Results: A total of 146 patients were analysed; 75.3% were male, with a mean age of 60.7 years. HPV positivity (p16+) was detected in 62.3%. All patients underwent radiotherapy, with 82.8% receiving concurrent chemoradiotherapy. The 5-year overall survival was 60.9% [95% confidence interval (CI): 52.7–70.3]. p16+ [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.19–0.68; p < 0.01] was independently associated with improved survival, whereas a smoking history of ≥ 10 pack-years (HR = 2.18; p = 0.02) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 2–4 (HR = 3.30; p < 0.01) were linked to worse outcomes. Conclusions: Survival outcomes in this South American population, with a high prevalence of HPV-associated OPSCC, were comparable to internationally published data. In exploratory analyses, HPV association and concurrent chemotherapy were associated with better survival outcomes, with no significant differences between cisplatin schedules. Article Open Access - Authors: - Article Number: 6|Published online on: November 12, 2026https://doi.org/10.3892/etm.2026.13354 - Expand metrics + The aim of the present study was to investigate variations in vaginal microecology across female populations, elucidate alterations in vaginal microecology across age groups and physiological states, and provide evidence to support clinical prevention, diagnosis and treatment of vaginal diseases to safeguard women's reproductive health. A total of 200 women who underwent routine health check‐ups at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Jinzhou Medical University between March and September 2024 were enrolled. According to age, subjects were divided into five groups: Group A (21‐29 years, n=40), Group B (30‐39 years, n=40), Group C (40‐49 years, n=40), Group D (50‐59 years, n=40), and Group E (≥60 years, n=40). Based on maternal status, the participants were categorized into a pregnant/postpartum group (defined as women during pregnancy or within 6 weeks postpartum, n=40) and a non‐pregnant/non‐postpartum group (women not in pregnancy or postpartum, n=40). Within the same age group, subjects were further divided into the vaginal disease group (women with vaginal diseases, n=40) and the healthy group (women with no vaginal diseases, n=40). All participants underwent tests including vaginal pH measurement, bacterial community analysis, vaginal microecological functional assays, and HPV detection. Indicators of pH, flora structure, and functional test results were compared among different age groups, maternal statuses, and disease states. The correlation between vaginal microecology and HPV infection was analyzed. title_original: Vaginal microecological characteristics in women across different age, maternal and disease states and their correlation with HPV infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate variations in vaginal microecology across female populations, elucidate alterations in vaginal microecology across age groups and physiological states, and provide evidence to support clinical prevention, diagnosis and treatment of vaginal diseases to safeguard women's reproductive health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A total of 200 women who underwent routine health check-ups at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Jinzhou Medical University between March and September 2024 were enrolled. Subjects were divided into five age groups (21-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, ≥60 years), a pregnant/postpartum group and a non-pregnant/non-postpartum group, and further categorized into a vaginal disease group and a healthy group within the same age group.
analysis.methods: All participants underwent tests including vaginal pH measurement, bacterial community analysis, vaginal microecological functional assays, and HPV detection. Indicators of pH, flora structure, and functional test results were compared among different age groups, maternal statuses, and disease states.
analysis.main_results: The correlation between vaginal microecology and HPV infection was analyzed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as providing evidence to support clinical prevention, diagnosis and treatment of vaginal diseases to safeguard women's reproductive health.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted clinical strategies for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of HPV-associated vaginal diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and the lack of detailed statistical analysis, but the evidence is moderate in strength due to the clear focus on HPV infection and its correlation with vaginal microecology.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates variations in vaginal microecology across different age groups, maternal statuses, and disease states, with a focus on their correlation with HPV infection. The research was conducted on 200 women at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Jinzhou Medical University between March and September 2024, divided into five age groups, a pregnant/postpartum group, and a non-pregnant/non-postpartum group, with further categorization into vaginal disease and healthy groups. Methods included vaginal pH measurement, bacterial community analysis, functional assays, and HPV detection. The study aimed to provide evidence for clinical prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of vaginal diseases related to HPV. The findings suggest a correlation between vaginal microecology and HPV infection, which could inform targeted clinical strategies for managing HPV-associated conditions. However, the study's observational design and lack of detailed statistical analysis limit the confidence in its conclusions, resulting in a moderate evidence strength assessment.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查女性人群阴道微生态的变化,阐明不同年龄组和生理状态下阴道微生态的变化,为阴道疾病的临床预防、诊断和治疗提供证据,保障女性生殖健康。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 纳入2024年3月至2024年9月期间在锦州医科大学第三附属医院进行常规健康检查的200名女性。将受试者分为5个年龄组(21-29岁、30-39岁、40-49岁、50-59岁、≥60岁)、孕/产后组和非孕/非产后组,并在同一年龄组内进一步分为阴道疾病组和健康组。
elements_zh.methods: 所有参与者均接受了阴道pH测量、细菌群落分析、阴道微生态功能测定和HPV检测等测试。比较不同年龄组、孕产妇状况和疾病状态之间的pH、菌群结构和功能测试结果等指标。
elements_zh.main_results: 分析阴道微生态与HPV感染的相关性。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,这些发现为支持阴道疾病的临床预防、诊断和治疗、保障女性生殖健康提供了证据。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为制定预防 HPV 相关阴道疾病、诊断 和 治疗 的针对性临床策略提供参考。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其观察性设计和缺乏详细的统计分析而受到限制,但由于明确关注 HPV 感染及其与阴道微生态的相关性,证据强度适中。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查女性人群阴道微生态的变化,阐明不同年龄组和生理状态下阴道微生态的变化,为阴道疾病的临床预防、诊断和治疗提供证据,保障女性生殖健康。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 纳入2024年3月至2024年9月期间在锦州医科大学第三附属医院进行常规健康检查的200名女性。将受试者分为5个年龄组(21-29岁、30-39岁、40-49岁、50-59岁、≥60岁)、孕/产后组和非孕/非产后组,并在同一年龄组内进一步分为阴道疾病组和健康组。
analysis_zh.methods: 所有参与者均接受了阴道pH测量、细菌群落分析、阴道微生态功能测定和HPV检测等测试。比较不同年龄组、孕产妇状况和疾病状态之间的pH、菌群结构和功能测试结果等指标。
analysis_zh.main_results: 分析阴道微生态与HPV感染的相关性。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,这些发现为支持阴道疾病的临床预防、诊断和治疗、保障女性生殖健康提供了证据。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为制定预防 HPV 相关阴道疾病、诊断 和 治疗 的针对性临床策略提供参考。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其观察性设计和缺乏详细的统计分析而受到限制,但由于明确关注 HPV 感染及其与阴道微生态的相关性,证据强度适中。

full_text: Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is necessary but not sufficient for cervical cancer, which caused approximately 350,000 deaths in 2022. Co-infections with Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and HIV may modify cervical carcinogenesis, but causal inference is constrained by confounding, study heterogeneity, and limited mechanistic validation in human tissue. This systematic integrative review (PRISMA 2020) searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (January 2015 to March 2026); risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. HIV co-infection shows the strongest evidence: approximately 6-fold risk elevation, a confirmed CD4 dose-response, and residual risk that persists despite antiretroviral therapy (GRADE: high). CT is associated with 2-4-fold elevations in observational studies, but substantial heterogeneity, residual sexual-behavior confounding, funnel-plot asymmetry suggesting publication bias, and attenuation of the HPV-adjusted independent effect (OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.03-3.01) leave causality uncertain (GRADE: Low-Moderate). HSV-2 associations are inconsistent: pooled cervical cancer risk was elevated (OR 3.01, 95% CI 2.24-4.04), but most estimates were unadjusted for HPV status, prospective studies are non-significant, and mechanistic evidence derives from non-human models (GRADE: low). A context-dependent syndemic effect appears in HIV co-infected populations. In conclusion, HIV meets criteria for a probable causal modifier of HPV-driven carcinogenesis, supporting WHO-endorsed intensified screening for women living with HIV; CT’s role remains uncertain pending rigorous confounder control; and HSV-2 does not meet the threshold for independent co-factor classification. Priorities include prospective cohorts and human cervical-tissue mechanistic validation. 2Materials and methods2.1Protocol, registration, and reporting standardsThis systematic integrative review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines (Page et al., 2021) and the integrative review methodology of Whittemore and Knafl (2005). The review protocol, including the pre-specified search strategy, inclusion criteria, and analysis methods, was developed in advance and followed consistently throughout the review. The protocol was not formally registered on PROSPERO or an equivalent registry; this is noted as a limitation in Section 10.2.2Search strategy2.2.1Databases, date range, and language restrictionFive databases were systematically searched: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. Supplementary grey literature sources included WHO reports, IARC monographs, GLOBOCAN 2022, and CDC/WHO STI and HIV guidelines. The last search was conducted in March 2026. The primary date range was January 2015 to March 2026; seminal pre-2015 studies were selectively included. The search was restricted to English-language publications, which may systematically under-represent data from high-burden regions where relevant research is published in other languages. The direction and magnitude of this potential bias cannot be determined.2.2.2Boolean search stringsHPV–CT: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“Chlamydia trachomatis” OR “chlamydial infection”) AND (“co-infection” OR “coinfection” OR “risk factor” OR “cervical carcinogenesis”)HPV–HSV-2: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“herpes simplex virus 2” OR “HSV-2”) AND (“co-infection” OR “carcinogenesis” OR “risk factor”)HPV–HIV: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“HIV” OR “human immunodeficiency virus” OR “women living with HIV”) AND (“co-infection” OR “cervical carcinogenesis” OR “antiretroviral” OR “CD4” OR “immunosuppression”)MeSH terms applied: Papillomaviridae; Uterine Cervical Neoplasms; Chlamydia trachomatis; Simplexvirus; HIV Infections; Coinfection; Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia; Carcinogenesis; Immune Evasion; Cytokines.The conceptual search logic above was translated into the native syntax of each database searched, using identical concepts, Boolean structure, and filters (Humans; English language; publication date 2015/01–2026/03) throughout. Full strings and yields are given below.2.2.3Database-specific search strings2.2.3.1PubMed/MEDLINE (native interface; searched directly)HPV–CT: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“Chlamydia trachomatis”[tiab] OR “chlamydial infection”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “coinfection”[tiab] OR “risk factor”[tiab] OR “cervical carcinogenesis”[tiab]), 204 records. HPV–HSV-2: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“herpes simplex virus 2”[tiab] OR “HSV-2”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “carcinogenesis”[tiab] OR “risk factor”[tiab]), 64 records. HPV–HIV: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“HIV”[tiab] OR “human immunodeficiency virus”[tiab] OR “women living with HIV”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “cervical carcinogenesis”[tiab] OR “antiretroviral”[tiab] OR “CD4”[tiab] OR “immunosuppression”[tiab]), 1,950 records.2.2.3.2Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane LibraryThe same conceptual logic was translated into each platform’s native syntax (Embase:.mp./Emtree; Scopus: TITLE-ABS-KEY(); Web of Science: TS=(); Cochrane::ti,ab,kw). PubMed/MEDLINE returned 2,218 records across the three strings (204, 64, and 1,950 for CT, HSV-2, and HIV, respectively), and the four remaining databases returned 629 records combined, for a total of 2,847 records identified. Because most records from these four databases had already been retrieved by PubMed/MEDLINE, they contributed few unique records after the 743 duplicates were removed. The full cascade is reported in Section 2.4 and Figure 1.Figure 1PRISMA 2020 flow diagram documenting the identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies for this systematic integrative review (flow counts shown in diagram).PRISMA-style flowchart outlining the systematic review process, showing stages of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. Database and supplementary source records are screened, with counts for duplicates and exclusions at each phase. Fifty-five studies are included in the narrative synthesis, categorized by type, and the total referenced studies, including contextual references, is seventy-four.2.3Eligibility criteria2.3.1Inclusion criteria (PICO-structured)Population: Women with confirmed HPV infection or at cervical cancer risk; all ages; all geographic settings. Exposure: Co-infection with CT, HSV-2, HIV, or multiple STIs concurrent with HPV. Comparator: HPV mono-infection; HIV-negative women; women without the specified STI. Outcomes: HPV persistence; CIN grades 1–3; invasive cervical cancer; molecular endpoints including cytokine profiles, viral load, and biomarker expression. Study designs: Cohort, case–control, cross-sectional, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and mechanistic in vitro/in vivo studies.2.3.2Exclusion criteriaStudies exclusively examining non-cervical HPV disease; observational studies with sample sizes below 50 (unless providing unique mechanistic data); case reports and editorials without primary data; and reviews published before 2010 unless of seminal historical importance.2.4Study selection and data extractionThe primary reviewer conducted systematic screening of titles, abstracts, and full-text articles. All inclusion decisions, borderline exclusions, and extracted data were independently verified by a second author, with disagreements resolved by consensus. This sequential verification protocol, although not equivalent to fully independent concurrent dual screening (the PRISMA 2020 standard), substantially reduces selection bias. Inter-rater reliability statistics were not calculated given the sequential design.PRISMA flow summary: 2,847 records were identified across the five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, n = 2,218; Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, n = 629 combined)); 743 duplicates were removed; 2,104 records were screened; 1,960 were excluded at the abstract stage; 144 full texts were assessed for eligibility; and 89 were excluded (insufficient co-infection data, n = 31; outcomes unavailable, n = 28; insufficient quality, n = 30). In total, 54 studies were included in the narrative synthesis (Figure 1): 18 on CT-HPV co-infection, 9 on HSV-2–HPV, 13 on HIV–HPV, and 14 on triple co-infection or cross-cutting themes. The 54 included sources refer to studies identified through the systematic search and eligibility process; an additional 21 references cited for background context, methodological frameworks, and clinical guidelines are not included in this count (75 total references).2.5Data extractionStandardized data extraction captured: author, year, country, study design, sample size, demographics, STI confirmation method (serological versus NAAT), HPV genotyping methodology, effect estimates (OR, HR, RR with 95% CI), follow-up duration, confounders adjusted, and quality score. Mechanistic studies additionally documented experimental model, cell line or species, intervention, replication evidence, and molecular endpoints. Heterogeneity statistics (I2 where reported) were recorded.2.6Risk of bias and mechanistic study assessmentObservational studies were assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS; 9-point: scores 7–9, high quality; 4–6, moderate; below 4, low). ROBINS-I was applied to non-randomized cohort designs. The GRADE framework was applied to all key epidemiological claims; a full evidence profile is presented in Table 1. Risk of bias was evaluated at the domain level across four dimensions: (1) selection bias, including the appropriateness of case and control source populations and non-participation bias in case–control designs; (2) exposure assessment bias, including serological versus NAAT-based STI detection and the misclassification implications of each; (3) confounding, including the completeness of sexual behavior covariate adjustment and the use of objective versus self-reported confounder measurement; and (4) outcome bias, including the consistency of cervical outcome ascertainment across study populations. Studies scoring below 5 on NOS are designated high risk of bias; studies with NOS 5–6 are moderate risk; NOS 7–9 are low risk. High-risk studies include the Ferrera et al. (2023) and Ngombe Mouabata et al. (2024) cross-sectional datasets, which provide important geographic representation but have limited adjustment for confounding. Sensitivity interpretation excluding these high-risk studies does not materially alter the primary conclusions for CT: the association with CIN and cervical cancer risk persists in higher-quality prospective and pooled case–control designs, though the effect size is attenuated. For HSV-2, the available studies consist predominantly of case–control designs (moderate-to-high bias risk arising from exposure and selection domains), and exclusion of these would leave an evidence base of two higher-quality studies (Lehtinen et al., 2002; The search was restricted to English-language publications, which may systematically under-represent data from high-burden regions where relevant research is published in other languages. The direction and magnitude of this potential bias cannot be determined.2.2.2Boolean search stringsHPV–CT: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“Chlamydia trachomatis” OR “chlamydial infection”) AND (“co-infection” OR “coinfection” OR “risk factor” OR “cervical carcinogenesis”)HPV–HSV-2: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“herpes simplex virus 2” OR “HSV-2”) AND (“co-infection” OR “carcinogenesis” OR “risk factor”)HPV–HIV: (“Human papillomavirus” OR “HPV” OR “cervical cancer” OR “CIN”) AND (“HIV” OR “human immunodeficiency virus” OR “women living with HIV”) AND (“co-infection” OR “cervical carcinogenesis” OR “antiretroviral” OR “CD4” OR “immunosuppression”)MeSH terms applied: Papillomaviridae; Uterine Cervical Neoplasms; Chlamydia trachomatis; Simplexvirus; HIV Infections; Coinfection; Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia; Carcinogenesis; Immune Evasion; Cytokines.The conceptual search logic above was translated into the native syntax of each database searched, using identical concepts, Boolean structure, and filters (Humans; English language; publication date 2015/01–2026/03) throughout. Full strings and yields are given below.2.2.3Database-specific search strings2.2.3.1PubMed/MEDLINE (native interface; searched directly)HPV–CT: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“Chlamydia trachomatis”[tiab] OR “chlamydial infection”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “coinfection”[tiab] OR “risk factor”[tiab] OR “cervical carcinogenesis”[tiab]), 204 records. HPV–HSV-2: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“herpes simplex virus 2”[tiab] OR “HSV-2”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “carcinogenesis”[tiab] OR “risk factor”[tiab]), 64 records. HPV–HIV: (“Human papillomavirus”[tiab] OR “HPV”[tiab] OR “cervical cancer”[tiab] OR “CIN”[tiab]) AND (“HIV”[tiab] OR “human immunodeficiency virus”[tiab] OR “women living with HIV”[tiab]) AND (“co-infection”[tiab] OR “cervical carcinogenesis”[tiab] OR “antiretroviral”[tiab] OR “CD4”[tiab] OR “immunosuppression”[tiab]), 1,950 records.2.2.3.2Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane LibraryThe same conceptual logic was translated into each platform’s native syntax (Embase:.mp./Emtree; Scopus: TITLE-ABS-KEY(); Web of Science: TS=(); Cochrane::ti,ab,kw). PubMed/MEDLINE returned 2,218 records across the three strings (204, 64, and 1,950 for CT, HSV-2, and HIV, respectively), and the four remaining databases returned 629 records combined, for a total of 2,847 records identified. Because most records from these four databases had already been retrieved by PubMed/MEDLINE, they contributed few unique records after the 743 duplicates were removed. The full cascade is reported in Section 2.4 and Figure 1.Figure 1PRISMA 2020 flow diagram documenting the identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies for this systematic integrative review (flow counts shown in diagram).PRISMA-style flowchart outlining the systematic review process, showing stages of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. Database and supplementary source records are screened, with counts for duplicates and exclusions at each phase. Fifty-five studies are included in the narrative synthesis, categorized by type, and the total referenced studies, including contextual references, is seventy-four.2.3Eligibility criteria2.3.1Inclusion criteria (PICO-structured)Population: Women with confirmed HPV infection or at cervical cancer risk; all ages; all geographic settings. Exposure: Co-infection with CT, HSV-2, HIV, or multiple STIs concurrent with HPV. Comparator: HPV mono-infection; HIV-negative women; women without the specified STI. Outcomes: HPV persistence; CIN grades 1–3; invasive cervical cancer; molecular endpoints including cytokine profiles, viral load, and biomarker expression. Study designs: Cohort, case–control, cross-sectional, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and mechanistic in vitro/in vivo studies.2.3.2Exclusion criteriaStudies exclusively examining non-cervical HPV disease; observational studies with sample sizes below 50 (unless providing unique mechanistic data); case reports and editorials without primary data; and reviews published before 2010 unless of seminal historical importance.2.4Study selection and data extractionThe primary reviewer conducted systematic screening of titles, abstracts, and full-text articles. All inclusion decisions, borderline exclusions, and extracted data were independently verified by a second author, with disagreements resolved by consensus. This sequential verification protocol, although not equivalent to fully independent concurrent dual screening (the PRISMA 2020 standard), substantially reduces selection bias. Inter-rater reliability statistics were not calculated given the sequential design.PRISMA flow summary: 2,847 records were identified across the five databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, n = 2,218; Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, n = 629 combined)); 743 duplicates were removed; 2,104 records were screened; 1,960 were excluded at the abstract stage; 144 full texts were assessed for eligibility; and 89 were excluded (insufficient co-infection data, n = 31; outcomes unavailable, n = 28; insufficient quality, n = 30). In total, 54 studies were included in the narrative synthesis (Figure 1): 18 on CT-HPV co-infection, 9 on HSV-2–HPV, 13 on HIV–HPV, and 14 on triple co-infection or cross-cutting themes. The 54 included sources refer to studies identified through the systematic search and eligibility process; an additional 21 references cited for background context, methodological frameworks, and clinical guidelines are not included in this count (75 total references).2.5Data extractionStandardized data extraction captured: author, year, country, study design, sample size, demographics, STI confirmation method (serological versus NAAT), HPV genotyping methodology, effect estimates (OR, HR, RR with 95% CI), follow-up duration, confounders adjusted, and quality score. Mechanistic studies additionally documented experimental model, cell line or species, intervention, replication evidence, and molecular endpoints. Heterogeneity statistics (I2 where reported) were recorded.2.6Risk of bias and mechanistic study assessmentObservational studies were assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS; 9-point: scores 7–9, high quality; 4–6, moderate; below 4, low). ROBINS-I was applied to non-randomized cohort designs. The GRADE framework was applied to all key epidemiological claims; a full evidence profile is presented in Table 1. full_text_sections.results: 3.1.2Meta-analytic findings and heterogeneityZhu et al. (2016) synthesized 22 studies comprising 4,291 cervical cancer cases and reported that CT infection is associated with elevated cervical cancer risk in prospective studies (OR = 2.21, 95% CI 1.88–2.61). HPV/CT co-infection was associated with an OR of 4.03 (95% CI 3.15–5.16) relative to no infection. However, heterogeneity was substantial across included studies (I2 significant), and the OR for CT as an independent predictor after HPV adjustment attenuated to 1.76 (95% CI 1.03–3.01), with the lower confidence bound approaching unity. This attenuation illustrates progressive confounder-driven reduction in effect size across studies with more rigorous adjustment (Figure 3).Naldini et al. (2019), in a meta-analysis of 48 studies, reported that among CT-positive women, the OR for any HPV infection was 2.12 (95% CI 1.80–2.49) and for HR-HPV specifically was 2.32 (95% CI 2.02–2.65). Conversely, the OR for CT infection among HPV-positive women was 2.23 (95% CI 1.70–2.92), confirming a bidirectional risk relationship with implications for co-screening strategies. Bhuvanendran Pillai et al. (2022) corroborated this risk elevation in a geographically diverse synthesis, noting that effect estimates were attenuated in studies employing NAAT-based CT detection versus serological methods, highlighting misclassification bias as a source of heterogeneity. Ji et al. (2019) reported CT co-infection in 8.4% of HPV-positive women from Inner Mongolia (n > 25,000), with co-infected women demonstrating significantly higher CIN2+ rates relative to HPV mono-infected women, extending the evidence base to East Asian populations underrepresented in European and North American meta-analyses (Figures 3, 4).Figure 3Forest plot of all published CT–HPV co-infection effect estimates for cervical neoplasia outcomes (Section 3). Log scale; box size proportional to study weight; dashed line = null (OR 1.0). Color coding: blue = systematic review/meta-analysis; green = prospective cohort; orange = IARC case-control; red = null or attenuated estimate after HPV/behavior adjustment. The Naldini et al. (2019) meta-analysis presents three bidirectional estimates; the Zhu et al. (2016) HPV-adjusted estimate is shown in red. OR, odds ratio; HR-HPV, high-risk HPV; CC, cervical cancer; MA, meta-analysis.Forest plot illustrating odds ratios with ninety-five percent confidence intervals for different studies on cervical neoplasia risk associated with HPV and chlamydia trachomatis, categorized by study type with color coding for meta-analyses, case-control, geographic cohort, and null associations after adjustment.Figure 4CT–HPV co-infection effect estimates ordered by descending OR magnitude (Section 3). Error bars = 95% CI. The gradient from co-infection OR (4.03) → pooled meta-analytic OR (~2.1–2.3) → IARC-adjusted (1.80) → HPV-adjusted independent CT effect (1.76) → null (1.00–1.10) illustrates progressive confounder-driven attenuation. OR, odds ratio; SCC, squamous cell carcinoma.Bar chart showing odds ratios with con!dence intervals from multiple studies on CT-HPV co-infection effect estimates for cervical neoplasia outcomes, categorized by study type using colorcoding; the null value is marked at one, and effect sizes generally attenuate with adjustment. 3.1.5Contradictory and null findingsSeveral studies report attenuation or loss of statistical significance after more stringent sexual behavior adjustment. Viikki et al. (2000) found no significant CT association after adjustment for HPV and number of sexual partners. Re-analyses incorporating more comprehensive sexual history data in European cohorts have similarly shown attenuated associations. These null findings raise the substantive possibility that a portion of the observed CT–cancer association reflects residual confounding by sexual behavior rather than an independent CT effect. Conversely, Shew et al. (2013) identified a biologically distinct pathway: CT detection was associated with redetection of HPV after apparent virological clearance, suggesting that CT may impair durable HPV immune control rather than directly promoting carcinogenesis de novo. This redetection mechanism, if confirmed in larger cohorts, offers a mechanistically coherent explanation that does not depend solely on direct oncogenic co-operation. 4.1.3Contradictory and null findingsMultiple cohort analyses have found no significant association between HSV-2 seropositivity and cervical cancer risk after adjustment for HPV and sexual partners. Tran-Thanh et al. (2003) detected no HSV-2 DNA by PCR in 200 cervical cancer specimens, arguing directly against persistent HSV-2 presence as a mechanism. Muwonga Tukisadila et al. (2025), studying female sex workers, reported that triple co-infection (HPV/HIV/HSV-2) was associated with elevated HPV16/18 viral load compared with dual or mono-infection. While not attributable to HSV-2 alone, this provides preliminary evidence that HSV-2 may exert a context-dependent co-promotional effect on HPV replication specifically when HIV-associated immune suppression is additionally present, a hypothesis distinct from HSV-2 acting as an independent carcinogen in immunocompetent women.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 11ConclusionsThe cumulative evidence supports HIV as a probable biological modifier of HPV-driven cervical carcinogenesis, with high certainty. CT is associated with elevated cervical cancer risk in observational studies, but causal classification remains provisional pending resolution of residual confounding, between-study heterogeneity, and the absence of human cervical tissue mechanistic validation. HSV-2 does not currently meet the evidentiary threshold for independent causal co-factor classification.For WLHIV, the evidence is most compelling: approximately 6-fold elevated cervical cancer risk, a dose–response relationship with CD4 count, partially validated immune mechanisms, and risk reduction (though not elimination) with ART collectively constitute the strongest available evidence base (GRADE: high). WHO 2021 guideline-endorsed intensified screening from age 25, multi-dose HPV vaccination, and screen-and-treat approaches represent appropriately evidence-grounded clinical standards.For CT, associated risk elevation in most observational studies is mechanistically coherent but constrained by high residual confounding risk, case–control design dominance, and limited human tissue mechanistic validation (GRADE: Low–Moderate). CT is associated with increased cervical cancer risk in observational data, but causality remains uncertain given residual confounding, substantial heterogeneity, and the attenuation of the HPV-adjusted independent effect toward the null. CT should not be characterized as a confirmed independent co-factor pending prospective validation with rigorous sexual behavior adjustment.For HSV-2, inconsistent epidemiological findings, absent viral genomic evidence in cancer tissue, and lack of mechanistic validation in human cervical tissue preclude causal classification (GRADE: low). Clinical practice should not be modified based on HSV-2 serostatus alone.Three research priorities emerge: (1) prospective longitudinal cohort studies with contemporaneous molecular co-infection monitoring, adequate power for sexual behavior adjustment, and pre-specified HPV clearance and CIN progression endpoints; (2) intervention studies testing CT treatment as a cervical cancer prevention strategy in randomized or quasi-experimental designs with HPV-adjusted endpoints; and (3) human cervical tissue mechanistic validation using ex vivo tissue and organoid systems, prioritizing the CT Pgp3–E6 pathway and HIV Tat transactivation.The global cervical cancer burden, concentrated in populations with the highest STI co-infection prevalence, makes integration of STI management and cervical cancer prevention programs a coherent public health priority. The precise magnitude of the prevention benefit attributable to broader STI management, however, requires prospective evidence that does not yet exist.
full_text_sections.other: 1Introduction1.1Global burden of cervical cancerCervical cancer affects approximately 660,000 women annually, with an estimated 350,000 deaths in 2022 (GLOBOCAN), making it the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide and the leading cause of cancer-related death in 23 low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) (Bray et al., 2024). Approximately 94% of deaths occur in LMICs, where vaccine coverage, screening access, and treatment availability remain inadequate (World Health Organization, 2023a). Age-standardized incidence in Eastern Africa exceeds 40 per 100,000, compared with fewer than 5 per 100,000 in Western Europe (Sung et al., 2021). Earlier GLOBOCAN data estimated 528,000 new cases in 2012, illustrating the persistent pre-elimination burden (Torre et al., 2015). Temporal trend analyses project increasing incidence in several high-burden LMICs absent accelerated intervention (Shao et al., 2026). Modeling analyses demonstrate that achieving the WHO 90–70–90 targets would avert up to 13.4 million cervical cancer cases by 2069 across 78 LMICs (Brisson et al., 2020). Global first-dose HPV vaccine coverage stands at approximately 27%, well below the elimination target (Han et al., 2025). HIV co-infection carries the single largest relative risk elevation of the three STIs considered here, detailed fully in Section 5.1.1.1.2HPV natural history and carcinogenesisHPV comprises over 200 genotypes, of which approximately 14 are classified as high-risk by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) (Muñoz et al., 2003). HPV-16 and HPV-18 together account for approximately 70–76% of invasive cervical cancers. In approximately 90% of infected women, HPV is cleared immunologically within 12–24 months (Rodriguez et al., 2008). Persistent infection is associated with constitutive E6 and E7 oncoprotein expression following viral genome integration and disruption of the E2 regulatory gene (Soheili et al., 2021; Kobayashi et al., 2024). E6 promotes p53 degradation and telomerase activation; E7 inactivates the retinoblastoma protein (pRb) (Mirabello et al., 2017; Rosendo-Chalma et al., 2024). High conservation of E7 sequences across HPV-16 strains is directly linked to oncogenic potency (Mirabello et al., 2017; Rosendo-Chalma et al., 2024). These molecular events underlie sustained proliferation, apoptosis resistance, and genomic instability over a typically 10–20-year progression interval (Schiffman et al., 2016). The local cervicovaginal microbiome and immune microenvironment also shape this trajectory, a theme returned to in Section 7.2.1.3The polymicrobial context of STIsSTIs co-occur frequently owing to shared behavioral risk factors. The WHO estimates 374 million new curable STI infections annually (World Health Organization, 2023b). CT accounts for approximately 128 million new infections per year; HSV-2 affects an estimated 13.2% of persons aged 15–49 globally (James et al., 2020); and HIV affects approximately 39 million people worldwide (UNAIDS, 2023). In the Middle East and Gulf region, reported STI prevalence probably underestimates true burden owing to ascertainment bias from stigma, limited surveillance, and restricted care-seeking (Akbari et al., 2023).1.4Rationale and objectivesDespite the recognized association between STI co-infection and cervical cancer outcomes, no methodologically rigorous integrative synthesis simultaneously addresses epidemiological magnitude, heterogeneity (including null findings), mechanistic plausibility with explicit evidence-level characterization, and clinically actionable guidance linked to evidence strength. full_text_excerpt: Co-infections with Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and HIV may modify cervical carcinogenesis, but causal inference is constrained by confounding, study heterogeneity, and limited mechanistic validation in human tissue. This systematic integrative review (PRISMA 2020) searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (January 2015 to March 2026); risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. In conclusion, HIV meets criteria for a probable causal modifier of HPV-driven carcinogenesis, supporting WHO-endorsed intensified screening for women living with HIV; CT’s role remains uncertain pending rigorous confounder control; and HSV-2 does not meet the threshold for independent co-factor classification. 2Materials and methods2.1Protocol, registration, and reporting standardsThis systematic integrative review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines (Page et al., 2021) and the integrative review methodology of Whittemore and Knafl (2005). The review protocol, including the pre-specified search strategy, inclusion criteria, and analysis methods, was developed in advance and followed consistently throughout the review. Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is necessary but not sufficient for cervical cancer, which caused approximately 350,000 deaths in 2022. HIV co-infection shows the strongest evidence: approximately 6-fold risk elevation, a confirmed CD4 dose-response, and residual risk that persists despite antiretroviral therapy (GRADE: high). Caution regarding ‘HPV status fully mediates sex-related survival differences in oropharyngeal cancer: a population-based analysis with formal interaction testing’. J Laryngol Otol 2026;1–2. https://doi.org/ 10.1017/S002221512610663X Received: 11 September 2026 UTC Revised: 11 September 2026 UTC Accepted: 17 September 2026 UTC Corresponding author: Adam Garrard; Email: adam.garrard@nhs.net © The Author(s), 2026. Published by Cambridge University Press on behalf of J.L.O. (1984) LIMITED. Caution regarding ‘HPV status fully mediates sex-related survival differences in oropharyngeal cancer: a population-based analysis with formal interaction testing’ Adam Garrard , Thomas Hampton and Andrew Lau Manchester Royal Infirmary, UK Dear Editors, We read with great interest the recent article by Hoenle et al., ‘HPV status fully mediates sex- related survival differences in oropharyngeal cancer: a population-based analysis with formal interaction testing’.1 The authors should be commended for addressing an important clinical question in a large contemporary population-based cohort. Their rationale is compelling, and the attempt to explore formally the relationship between sex, p16 and/or human papillomavirus (HPV) status and survival represents a valuable contribution to the literature. We would, however, urge caution in concluding that HPV status ‘fully and mechanistically’ explains apparent sex-related differences in survival, particularly when considering overall sur- vival. The principal limitation is inherent to the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) dataset. As the authors acknowledge, smoking history, performance status and co- morbidity data are unavailable.1 These are crucial prognostic determinants in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); their omission limits the extent to which differences in overall survival can be attributed independently to sex or HPV status. The importance of tobacco exposure is particularly well established. Platek et al. demon- strated that, among patients with oropharyngeal SCC treated with chemoradiotherapy, current smoking was associated with substantially increased mortality in both HPV-positive and HPV- negative disease.2 Furthermore, Ang et al. found smoking to be an independent and significant determinant of overall survival, with tobacco exposure contributing to their risk stratification of patients with HPV-positive disease.3 More recently, a meta-analysis of 15 studies of HPV- related oropharyngeal SCC found that ever-smokers had more than twice the mortality of never-smokers (hazard ratio 2.4), while current smoking was associated with a hazard ratio for overall mortality of 3.2.4 Smoking therefore represents more than simply an aetiological risk factor; it is an important prognostic variable even after HPV status has been established. Co-morbidity and baseline functional status are similarly relevant. Habbous et al. demon- strated that increasing Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with poorer overall survival in oropharyngeal cancer, including after adjustment for HPV status.5 Skillington et al. subsequently found 5-year overall survival of 71 per cent in patients with none-to- mild co-morbidity compared with 49 per cent in those with moderate-to-severe co-morbidity, and demonstrated particular prognostic importance of co-morbidity in p16-negative disease.6 Contemporary oropharyngeal SCC series have also demonstrated the importance of perfor- mance status. In a 2023 cohort, Embring et al. found both impaired performance status (hazard ratio 1.51) and current smoking (hazard ratio 2.57) to be independent adverse prognostic factors for overall survival alongside HPV status.7 Klasen et al. similarly identified Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status as a significant predictor of overall survival on multivariable analysis in their sex-specific oropharyngeal SCC cohort.8 Alcohol exposure may provide an additional source of residual confounding. Koyama et al., studying 2626 patients with oral and pharyngeal malignancies, reported increased all-cause mortality among heavy alcohol consumers after adjustment for smoking, stage, treatment and other co-variates; importantly, this association was observed in both men and women.9 Alcohol consumption has also been shown to differ according to sex in oropharyngeal SCC cohorts.8 Importantly, socioeconomic status has not been considered. Human papillomavirus-positive oropharyngeal SCC patients had higher rates of smoking and deprivation than the general Scottish population in a recent study, challenging the concept that HPV-positive oropharyn- geal SCC is not associated with these factors.10 We also know that socioeconomic deprivation is associated with incomplete radiotherapy treatment in head and neck cancer, potentially con- tributing to inequity in outcomes.11 Treatment interruptions may themselves negatively affect locoregional control and overall survival.12 https://doi.org/10.1017/S002221512610663X Downloaded from https://www.cambridge.org/core. IP address: 52.183.7.215, on 13 Nov 2026 at 23:21:55, subject to the Cambridge Core terms of use, available at https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. 2 Garrard et al. Although the reported findings cannot be considered ‘unambiguous’, we strongly support the authors’ calls for sex- disaggregated reporting in future de-escalation trials. We would further encourage studies of sex-related outcomes in oropharyn- geal SCC to consider the patient as a whole, rather than attributing observed differences primarily to tumour biology alone. Sex, HPV status, smoking, alcohol exposure, co-morbidity, performance sta- tus and socioeconomic circumstances may all influence treatment, including treatment completion and survival. Mixed-methods attempts to incorporate these behavioural, clinical and social determinants alongside tumour-specific characteristics may help optimise our patients’ treatment. Caution regarding ‘HPV status fully mediates sex-related survival differences in oropharyngeal cancer: a population-based analysis with formal interaction testing’ Adam Garrard , Thomas Hampton and Andrew Lau Manchester Royal Infirmary, UK Dear Editors, We read with great interest the recent article by Hoenle et al., ‘HPV status fully mediates sex- related survival differences in oropharyngeal cancer: a population-based analysis with formal interaction testing’.1 The authors should be commended for addressing an important clinical question in a large contemporary population-based cohort. Their rationale is compelling, and the attempt to explore formally the relationship between sex, p16 and/or human papillomavirus (HPV) status and survival represents a valuable contribution to the literature. We would, however, urge caution in concluding that HPV status ‘fully and mechanistically’ explains apparent sex-related differences in survival, particularly when considering overall sur- vival. The principal limitation is inherent to the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) dataset. As the authors acknowledge, smoking history, performance status and co- morbidity data are unavailable.1 These are crucial prognostic determinants in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); their omission limits the extent to which differences in overall survival can be attributed independently to sex or HPV status. The importance of tobacco exposure is particularly well established. Platek et al. demon- strated that, among patients with oropharyngeal SCC treated with chemoradiotherapy, current smoking was associated with substantially increased mortality in both HPV-positive and HPV- negative disease.2 Furthermore, Ang et al. found smoking to be an independent and significant determinant of overall survival, with tobacco exposure contributing to their risk stratification of patients with HPV-positive disease.3 More recently, a meta-analysis of 15 studies of HPV- related oropharyngeal SCC found that ever-smokers had more than twice the mortality of never-smokers (hazard ratio 2.4), while current smoking was associated with a hazard ratio for overall mortality of 3.2.4 Smoking therefore represents more than simply an aetiological risk factor; it is an important prognostic variable even after HPV status has been established. Co-morbidity and baseline functional status are similarly relevant. Habbous et al. demon- strated that increasing Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with poorer overall survival in oropharyngeal cancer, including after adjustment for HPV status.5 Skillington et al. subsequently found 5-year overall survival of 71 per cent in patients with none-to- mild co-morbidity compared with 49 per cent in those with moderate-to-severe co-morbidity, and demonstrated particular prognostic importance of co-morbidity in p16-negative disease.6 Contemporary oropharyngeal SCC series have also demonstrated the importance of perfor- mance status. In a 2023 cohort, Embring et al. found both impaired performance status (hazard ratio 1.51) and current smoking (hazard ratio 2.57) to be independent adverse prognostic factors for overall survival alongside HPV status.7 Klasen et al. similarly identified Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status as a significant predictor of overall survival on multivariable analysis in their sex-specific oropharyngeal SCC cohort.8 Alcohol exposure may provide an additional source of residual confounding. Koyama et al., studying 2626 patients with oral and pharyngeal malignancies, reported increased all-cause mortality among heavy alcohol consumers after adjustment for smoking, stage, treatment and other co-variates; importantly, this association was observed in both men and women.9 Alcohol consumption has also been shown to differ according to sex in oropharyngeal SCC cohorts.8 Importantly, socioeconomic status has not been considered. Human papillomavirus-positive oropharyngeal SCC patients had higher rates of smoking and deprivation than the general Scottish population in a recent study, challenging the concept that HPV-positive oropharyn- geal SCC is not associated with these factors.10 We also know that socioeconomic deprivation is associated with incomplete radiotherapy treatment in head and neck cancer, potentially con- tributing to inequity in outcomes.11 Treatment interruptions may themselves negatively affect locoregional control and overall survival.12 https://doi.org/10.1017/S002221512610663X Downloaded from https://www.cambridge.org/core. Although the reported findings cannot be considered ‘unambiguous’, we strongly support the authors’ calls for sex- disaggregated reporting in future de-escalation trials. We would further encourage studies of sex-related outcomes in oropharyn- geal SCC to consider the patient as a whole, rather than attributing observed differences primarily to tumour biology alone. Sex, HPV status, smoking, alcohol exposure, co-morbidity, performance sta- tus and socioeconomic circumstances may all influence treatment, including treatment completion and survival. Mixed-methods attempts to incorporate these behavioural, clinical and social determinants alongside tumour-specific characteristics may help optimise our patients’ treatment. full_text: BackgroundCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a rare subtype of malignant tumor. When it presents as pelvic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the difficulty of clinical diagnosis and treatment increases significantly. Notably, some such pelvic SCC cases are confirmed to be associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, yet the primary tumor remains unidentified despite systematic imaging evaluation, endoscopy, and pathological biopsy. Currently, there is no unified consensus on the diagnostic criteria, therapeutic strategies, and prognostic assessment of this specific clinical entity, which has become one of the urgent problems to be solved in oncology.Case presentationA 55-year-old postmenopausal woman was admitted with urinary discomfort and lower abdominal distension for 15 days. Physical examination revealed a fixed, non-tender solid pelvic mass in the left lower abdomen. Laboratory testing showed an elevated serum squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC-Ag) level of 9.11 ng/mL, while other tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 125, were within normal ranges. Transvaginal ultrasonography and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass in the left pelvis. To investigate the primary site, comprehensive evaluation including cervical HPV testing and cytology, colonoscopy, and cystoscopy was performed, but no definite primary malignant lesion was identified. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the pelvic mass showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Exploratory laparotomy was subsequently performed, and postoperative histopathological examination confirmed moderately to well-differentiated invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Diffuse strong p16 expression together with positive tumor HPV E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supported an HPV-associated tumor phenotype. Although lymph node metastasis was suspected intraoperatively, no definite lymph node metastasis was confirmed by pathological examination.ConclusionThis case describes a rare HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin in which no definite primary malignancy was identified in the cervix, other lower genital tract sites, gastrointestinal tract, or urinary tract after comprehensive evaluation. The case highlights the diagnostic value of integrating imaging, endoscopic assessment, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and tumor-based HPV testing in patients with pelvic SCC of uncertain origin. Importantly, the absence of a detectable mucosal primary site should not be interpreted as evidence of a primary pelvic origin. Instead, occult mucosal disease and other potential primary sites should remain diagnostic considerations. Further accumulation of similar cases and longer follow-up are needed to clarify the biological origin and optimal management of this rare clinical presentation. Patient perspectiveThe patient reported considerable anxiety after being informed that the pelvic mass was malignant, particularly because the primary site could not be identified and the extent of surgery was uncertain. She described relief after the operation when her urinary discomfort and lower abdominal distension improved and no major postoperative complications occurred. During subsequent chemotherapy and follow-up, she remained concerned about the possibility of recurrence but was reassured by the normalization of serum SCC-Ag and the absence of recurrent or metastatic disease on follow-up imaging. This section summarizes the patient’s perspective as reported during clinical care and follow-up. DiscussionMost malignant tumors have relatively definite primary sites with obvious localized or metastatic symptoms. Occult primary or CUP is defined as a malignant tumor for which the primary site cannot be determined after detailed history taking, complete physical examination (including pelvic and rectal examinations), laboratory tests (complete blood count, urinalysis, fecal occult blood), pathological examination with immunohistochemistry, chest X-ray, abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT), and mammography, endoscopy, or PET/CT scanning when necessary (3, 4). CUP accounts for approximately 2% of all invasive cancers, and only 30% of patients can be diagnosed with a primary site after pathological and biopsy evaluation (5). Reported subtypes include squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), adenocarcinoma, undifferentiated carcinoma, poorly differentiated tumor, and neuroendocrine tumor. As an HPV-associated SCC of unknown origin presenting in the pelvis, this case represents an exceptionally rare clinical presentation (1). Previous NCCN guidance for occult primary tumors recommended an evaluation incorporating pelvic/abdominal CT, gynecologic oncology consultation, anoscopy, and cystoscopy (5). In particular, PET and PET/CT have also been used in the evaluation of occult primary tumors (5). Preoperatively, the patient underwent FDG-PET without detection of an occult primary lesion. Gynecologic examination showed no abnormalities of the vulva, vagina, or cervix; cervical HPV testing and thin-prep cytology were negative; and colonoscopy, cystoscopy, and other auxiliary examinations showed no definite abnormalities. SCC-Ag was elevated, whereas the other tumor markers were negative.The differential diagnosis of HPV-associated pelvic SCC without an identifiable primary site requires systematic consideration of both gynecologic and non-gynecologic origins. In women, the cervix is an important potential source because cervical SCC is strongly associated with high-risk HPV; however, an occult cervical primary may occasionally be difficult to identify, particularly when no gross cervical lesion is present. In the present case, gynecologic examination showed a smooth cervix, cervical cytology was negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy, cervical HPV testing was negative, and postoperative histopathological examination of the entirely submitted cervix showed no squamous intraepithelial lesion or invasive cervical carcinoma. However, no additional serial or step sectioning was performed; therefore, an extremely small or regressed cervical primary cannot be completely excluded. Other HPV-associated mucosal sites, including the vagina, vulva, and anorectal region, were also considered. No suspicious vulvar or vaginal lesion was identified on examination, and colonoscopic evaluation revealed no colorectal mucosal malignancy. A urinary tract origin was considered because the pelvic tumor involved the bladder surface and the patient initially presented with urinary discomfort; however, cystoscopy demonstrated no intravesical mass or other mucosal lesion, favoring secondary involvement rather than a primary bladder tumor. The bilateral adnexa were macroscopically normal at surgery and showed no malignant involvement on pathological examination, arguing against an ovarian or tubal primary. PET/CT likewise failed to identify another primary lesion or distant metastatic disease. Taken together, the available findings supported classification as SCC of unknown primary origin. Nevertheless, an occult HPV-associated mucosal primary, particularly of cervical or other lower anogenital origin, cannot be definitively excluded.Notably, routine cervical HPV testing was negative, whereas the pelvic tumor showed diffuse p16 expression and positive HPV E6/E7 mRNA by in situ hybridization. Several factors may contribute to this apparent discordance. False-negative cervical HPV results may occur because of low viral load, sampling limitations, or differences in assay target coverage (6–8). In addition, integration of the HPV genome into host DNA may be accompanied by loss of certain viral genomic regions, whereas the E6/E7 oncogenes are more commonly retained and expressed (9–11). Other proposed explanations, including viral clearance or the theoretical “hit-and-run” mechanism, have also been discussed in HPV-associated carcinogenesis but remain speculative in the present case (12–15). Therefore, negative cervical HPV testing does not by itself exclude an HPV-associated malignancy when the tumor morphology and molecular findings raise suspicion. In this patient, the combination of squamous morphology, diffuse p16 expression, and positive tumor HPV E6/E7 mRNA supported an HPV-associated tumor phenotype despite negative cervical HPV testing.Pathological and molecular assessment is particularly important when pelvic SCC presents without an identifiable primary site. In the present case, CK5/6 and p40 positivity supported squamous differentiation, while diffuse strong p16 expression raised suspicion for an HPV-associated tumor. In HPV-associated malignancies, E7-mediated disruption of the pRb pathway results in compensatory p16 overexpression, although p16 alone is not entirely specific for transcriptionally active HPV infection (16–19). Therefore, tumor-based HPV testing may provide additional evidence when the anatomical primary remains uncertain. In this case, HPV E6/E7 mRNA was detected by in situ hybridization, providing more direct evidence of transcriptionally active HPV within the pelvic tumor (20, 21). Taken together, the histomorphological, immunohistochemical, and molecular findings supported classification of the lesion as an HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma, but did not establish its anatomical site of origin.Multiple studies have found that HPV-associated SCC can occur at various anatomical sites, and cervical SCC has long been regarded as the most common HPV-associated malignant tumor in women. In addition to the cervix, the vagina, vulva, and anus are also potential sites of HPV-associated SCC (22, 23). The therapeutic strategy in this case was influenced by the uncertainty regarding the primary site and by the anatomical extent of the pelvic lesion. Preoperatively, the mass was initially considered to be of ovarian origin on the basis of its pelvic location and imaging findings. Exploratory laparotomy was therefore undertaken to clarify the tumor origin and extent and to obtain definitive pathological assessment. Intraoperative exploration demonstrated grossly normal bilateral adnexa and an infiltrative left pelvic mass involving the pelvic sidewall and adjacent structures, prompting adjustment of the surgical procedure to total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, left pelvic lymphadenectomy, and para-aortic lymphadenectomy, with placement of a left ureteral stent. Postoperative pathological and molecular evaluation established HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma, while comprehensive assessment failed to identify a definite primary site. Given the squamous histology, pelvic distribution of disease, and absence of an established site-specific treatment pathway for this unusual presentation, postoperative systemic chemotherapy with paclitaxel plus cisplatin was administered. Serum SCC-Ag normalized after the first cycle, and three cycles were completed without severe adverse events. Further anticancer treatment was not pursued because of financial constraints, and the patient subsequently elected surveillance; radiotherapy was not administered. At approximately 11 months after surgery, follow-up CT showed no recurrent or metastatic disease and serum tumor markers remained within the normal range. Nevertheless, the relatively limited follow-up duration and the limited course of anticancer treatment should be considered when interpreting the apparent favorable short-term outcome. ConclusionIn summary, this case illustrates the diagnostic complexity of HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma when no primary site can be identified despite comprehensive evaluation. Tumor morphology, immunohistochemistry, and HPV E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supported an HPV-associated squamous phenotype, whereas gynecologic examination, cervical testing, imaging, endoscopic evaluation, and pathological assessment did not reveal a definite mucosal primary lesion. Accordingly, the tumor is best regarded as HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin rather than primary pelvic SCC. Occult cervical or other HPV-associated mucosal primary sites cannot be completely excluded, and an ectopic pelvic origin remains only a theoretical possibility that cannot be established from a single case. This case highlights the importance of multimodal diagnostic assessment and tumor-based HPV testing in the evaluation of pelvic SCC of uncertain origin. Additional cases and longer follow-up are needed to better define the biological origin and optimal management of this rare presentation. IntroductionCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a highly heterogeneous group of metastatic malignant tumors, defined as malignant tumors for which the primary site cannot be identified using standard imaging, endoscopic, and pathological biopsy at initial diagnosis (1). CUP accounts for approximately 1%–3% of all malignant tumors and is characterized by early widespread metastasis, non-specific clinical symptoms, and low sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy (2). Since treatment strategies are highly dependent on the identification of the primary site, the diagnosis and treatment of these cases pose great challenges.Approximately 5%–10% of CUP cases are pathologically classified as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). When SCC-CUP occurs in the pelvis, the core of differential diagnosis is to confirm whether it originates from mucosal sites such as the cervix, vagina, or anorectum, most of which are associated with high-risk HPV infection (1). Accordingly, p16 immunohistochemistry and tumor-based HPV testing may help characterize the HPV-associated phenotype of pelvic SCC. However, these findings alone cannot establish the anatomical site of origin. A rare diagnostic scenario may therefore arise in which an HPV-associated SCC presents in the pelvis despite the absence of an identifiable mucosal primary lesion.Herein, we report a rare case of HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin. Despite comprehensive evaluation, including gynecologic examination, cervical HPV testing and cytology, imaging, endoscopic assessment, and pathological examination, no definite mucosal primary lesion was identified. Tumor-based pathological and molecular findings supported an association with transcriptionally active HPV. This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges encountered when an HPV-associated SCC presents as a pelvic mass without an identifiable primary site. We therefore focus on the differential diagnosis, diagnostic reasoning, and therapeutic considerations of this unusual clinical presentation, while distinguishing the findings directly supported by this case from hypotheses regarding its possible site of origin. Case presentationA 55-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 4, para 3) with a history of ectopic pregnancy presented with no postmenopausal vaginal bleeding or contact bleeding. She had no previous history of cervical lesions and did not undergo regular cervical cancer screening. She denied medical, surgical, genetic, or familial malignant diseases. Fifteen days before admission to our institution, the patient developed urinary discomfort and lower abdominal distension and sought medical attention at a local hospital, where a pelvic mass was identified. 18F-FDG-PET/CT subsequently demonstrated an ill-defined soft-tissue mass in the left pelvis, measuring approximately 52 × 34 mm (Figure 1), with increased FDG uptake and close relationship to the pelvic wall muscles and left adnexa, suggestive of malignancy. Multiple enlarged retroperitoneal lymph nodes were present without abnormal FDG uptake, and no definite metastatic lesions were identified elsewhere. Transvaginal ultrasonography subsequently demonstrated a solid mass in the left adnexal region. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the mass then revealed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma without immunohistochemical testing. Gynecological examination showed smooth vulvar and vaginal mucosa; the cervix was 3 cm in diameter with a smooth surface; the uterine body was normal in size and shape; a solid mass of approximately 5 cm×5 cm was palpable on the left side of the uterus, non-tender, poorly mobile, with unclear boundaries from the pelvic wall; no abnormal mass or tenderness was detected in the right adnexal region. Serum SCC-Ag was 9.11 ng/mL (normal ≤2.7 ng/mL); other tumor markers including alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 125 (CA125), CA19-9, and β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) were within normal limits. Cervical HPV DNA genotyping was performed using a 37-genotype Human Papillomavirus Genotyping Detection Kit (PCR plus flow-through hybridization; Chaozhou Hybribio Biochemistry Co., Ltd., Chaozhou, China), covering HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 26, 31, 33, 34, 35, 39, 40, 42, 43, 44, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 61, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 81, 82, 83, and 84. All tested HPV genotypes were negative. ThinPrep cytologic testing (TCT) showed no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM).
