Intraoperative exploration demonstrated grossly normal bilateral adnexa and an infiltrative left pelvic mass involving the pelvic sidewall and adjacent structures, prompting adjustment of the surgical procedure to total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, left pelvic lymphadenectomy, and para-aortic lymphadenectomy, with placement of a left ureteral stent. Postoperative pathological and molecular evaluation established HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma, while comprehensive assessment failed to identify a definite primary site. Given the squamous histology, pelvic distribution of disease, and absence of an established site-specific treatment pathway for this unusual presentation, postoperative systemic chemotherapy with paclitaxel plus cisplatin was administered. Serum SCC-Ag normalized after the first cycle, and three cycles were completed without severe adverse events. Further anticancer treatment was not pursued because of financial constraints, and the patient subsequently elected surveillance; radiotherapy was not administered. At approximately 11 months after surgery, follow-up CT showed no recurrent or metastatic disease and serum tumor markers remained within the normal range. Nevertheless, the relatively limited follow-up duration and the limited course of anticancer treatment should be considered when interpreting the apparent favorable short-term outcome.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn summary, this case illustrates the diagnostic complexity of HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma when no primary site can be identified despite comprehensive evaluation. Tumor morphology, immunohistochemistry, and HPV E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supported an HPV-associated squamous phenotype, whereas gynecologic examination, cervical testing, imaging, endoscopic evaluation, and pathological assessment did not reveal a definite mucosal primary lesion. Accordingly, the tumor is best regarded as HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin rather than primary pelvic SCC. Occult cervical or other HPV-associated mucosal primary sites cannot be completely excluded, and an ectopic pelvic origin remains only a theoretical possibility that cannot be established from a single case. This case highlights the importance of multimodal diagnostic assessment and tumor-based HPV testing in the evaluation of pelvic SCC of uncertain origin. Additional cases and longer follow-up are needed to better define the biological origin and optimal management of this rare presentation.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a highly heterogeneous group of metastatic malignant tumors, defined as malignant tumors for which the primary site cannot be identified using standard imaging, endoscopic, and pathological biopsy at initial diagnosis (1). CUP accounts for approximately 1%–3% of all malignant tumors and is characterized by early widespread metastasis, non-specific clinical symptoms, and low sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy (2). Since treatment strategies are highly dependent on the identification of the primary site, the diagnosis and treatment of these cases pose great challenges.Approximately 5%–10% of CUP cases are pathologically classified as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). When SCC-CUP occurs in the pelvis, the core of differential diagnosis is to confirm whether it originates from mucosal sites such as the cervix, vagina, or anorectum, most of which are associated with high-risk HPV infection (1). Accordingly, p16 immunohistochemistry and tumor-based HPV testing may help characterize the HPV-associated phenotype of pelvic SCC. However, these findings alone cannot establish the anatomical site of origin. A rare diagnostic scenario may therefore arise in which an HPV-associated SCC presents in the pelvis despite the absence of an identifiable mucosal primary lesion.Herein, we report a rare case of HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin. Despite comprehensive evaluation, including gynecologic examination, cervical HPV testing and cytology, imaging, endoscopic assessment, and pathological examination, no definite mucosal primary lesion was identified. Tumor-based pathological and molecular findings supported an association with transcriptionally active HPV. This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges encountered when an HPV-associated SCC presents as a pelvic mass without an identifiable primary site. We therefore focus on the differential diagnosis, diagnostic reasoning, and therapeutic considerations of this unusual clinical presentation, while distinguishing the findings directly supported by this case from hypotheses regarding its possible site of origin. She had no previous history of cervical lesions and did not undergo regular cervical cancer screening. She denied medical, surgical, genetic, or familial malignant diseases. False-negative cervical HPV results may occur because of low viral load, sampling limitations, or differences in assay target coverage (6–8). Therefore, negative cervical HPV testing does not by itself exclude an HPV-associated malignancy when the tumor morphology and molecular findings raise suspicion. full_text: AbstractObjectiveGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (G-EAC) is a distinct human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma for which early diagnosis continues to pose a clinical challenge. We set out to characterize the clinical and sonographic features of G-EAC and to provide hypothesis-generating observations to guide future research.MethodsThis retrospective analysis comprised 13 patients with histopathologically confirmed G-EAC who underwent surgery at our center between August 2017 and September 2024. We reviewed and descriptively summarized the clinical presentation, HPV and cytology results, cervical biopsy findings, tumor markers, and ultrasonographic and cross-sectional imaging findings, together with all available pathological and surgical records.ResultsThe patients were aged 39–76 years (mean, 53.4 years), and all were parous. Vaginal discharge was the most common presenting symptom (8/13, 61.5%), followed by irregular vaginal bleeding (4/13, 30.8%) and postcoital bleeding (1/13, 7.7%). HPV testing was negative in 11/13 patients (84.6%); 1/13 (7.7%) tested positive for HPV 58, and another 1/13 (7.7%) carried a different high-risk HPV type. ThinPrep cytologic testing (TCT) was negative in 12/13 patients (92.3%), whereas atypical squamous cells were detected in 1/13 (7.7%). Among the 11 patients who underwent colposcopy with cervical biopsy, histopathological findings were negative in 8/11 (72.7%), mild glandular atypia was identified in 2/11 (18.2%), and rare adenocarcinoma cells were identified in 1/11 (9.1%). All 13 patients underwent preoperative ultrasound. Ultrasound findings raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in 9/13 patients (69.2%), were suggestive of benign cervical cystic lesions in 2/13 (15.4%), and were unremarkable in the remaining 2/13 (15.4%). A honeycomb sonographic pattern was present in 7/13 patients (53.8%), and abundant intralesional vascularity (Adler grade III) was present in 9/13 patients (69.2%). Preoperative MRI was performed in 10/13 patients (76.9%), 1 of whom also underwent CT, whereas the remaining 3/13 patients (23.1%) underwent neither MRI nor CT. A barrel-shaped cervix was documented in the pathological or surgical records of 4/13 patients (30.8%).ConclusionG-EAC may come to attention through a combination of clinical and imaging findings that together raise diagnostic suspicion. In this series, HPV negativity was common, and vaginal discharge was the most frequent presenting complaint. A honeycomb sonographic pattern and abundant intralesional vascularity may raise suspicion of G-EAC, although these findings remain descriptive and require validation in larger, adequately controlled studies.Keywords: gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma, honeycomb pattern, HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma, sonographic features, ultrasonography Materials and methodsGeneral dataWe retrospectively reviewed the clinical and imaging data of 13 patients with pathologically confirmed G-EAC who underwent surgery at our institution between August 2017 and September 2024. All patients were parous women aged 39–76 years (mean age, 53.4 years), and all 13 underwent preoperative transvaginal ultrasound. Preoperative MRI was performed in 10 patients, 1 of whom also underwent CT; the remaining 3 underwent neither modality. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) surgical treatment at our institution during the study period; (2) histopathological confirmation of G-EAC from biopsy, conization, or surgical specimens according to the 2020 WHO Classification; and (3) complete preoperative ultrasound data. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) receipt of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy before surgery; and (2) incomplete clinical or imaging data. Eligible patients were retrieved from the institutional pathology database. The follow-up cutoff was August 2026. The study protocol was approved by the Hospital Ethics Committee (Approval No. 2025-SY-096). Because of the retrospective design, the requirement for written informed consent was waived. All patient data and images were fully anonymized before analysis. Equipment and methodsEquipmentExaminations were performed with GE Voluson E10, Samsung HERA W10, and Mindray Resona 8 color Doppler ultrasound systems and endocavity probes operating at 5–10 MHz.Examination methodsAll 13 patients underwent preoperative transvaginal ultrasound. Patients were placed in the lithotomy position, and the uterus and bilateral adnexa were scanned systematically in multiple planes. When a cervical lesion was identified, its size, location, margins, and internal echogenicity were recorded. Intralesional and perilesional vascularity was assessed with color Doppler imaging. We categorized vascularity descriptively using the Adler grading framework (3): grade 0, no detectable color flow signals; grade I, one or two punctate persistent flow signals within the tumor (diameter <0.1 cm); grade II, multiple small vessels or a single dominant vessel; grade III, four or more distinct vessels within the lesion. Because of the retrospective design, detailed Doppler acquisition parameters (pulse-repetition frequency, color gain, and wall-filter settings) were not uniformly archived and could not be standardized. Continuous variables are summarized as mean (range) and categorical variables as frequencies (percentages). No inferential testing was undertaken, given the small sample size and the absence of any control group.Follow-upPostoperative follow-up data were collected from institutional medical records, and each patient's status was recorded as ongoing, lost to follow-up, or deceased. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (G-EAC) is an HPV-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma with distinct clinicopathological characteristics. Because the tumor is HPV-independent, HPV-based screening may remain negative, and a deep location within the endocervical canal and cervical stroma can further limit its detection by cytology and superficial cervical biopsy (6–9). In this retrospective descriptive series of 13 patients with pathologically confirmed G-EAC, the combined clinical, sonographic, cross-sectional imaging, and pathological findings illustrate why this uncommon tumor may be difficult to recognize before surgery. Persistent symptoms despite negative conventional screening, together with suspicious cervical imaging abnormalities, should prompt consideration of a deeply located glandular lesion that warrants further evaluation.Clinical and screening featuresIn our series, most patients tested negative on HPV testing, cytology, and colposcopic biopsy. These findings are in keeping with the HPV-independent biology of G-EAC and illustrate the limitations of conventional cervical screening and superficial biopsy for detecting lesions that lie deep within the endocervical canal (6–9). Negative HPV testing, cytology, or superficial cervical biopsy do not necessarily exclude an occult glandular malignancy when clinical or imaging findings remain suspicious.In our cohort, persistent vaginal discharge was the most frequent presenting symptom, followed by irregular vaginal bleeding and postcoital bleeding. Similar presentations have been reported in earlier studies of HPV-independent and gastric-type cervical adenocarcinoma (8, 10). Gastric-type and usual-type endocervical adenocarcinomas also differ in their clinicopathological and molecular characteristics (11). Because these symptoms are relatively nonspecific, they may not immediately suggest cervical malignancy, especially when routine cervical screening remains negative. Persistent or unexplained vaginal discharge or bleeding should likewise prompt further assessment when clinical examination or imaging findings raise concern about an underlying cervical lesion. In this series, tumor markers were elevated in only a minority of patients; given their nonspecific nature, they should be interpreted as adjunctive clinical information rather than as diagnostic findings.Sonographic characteristics and diagnostic pitfallsSonographic appearances of G-EAC varied considerably across this series. A honeycomb-like pattern, operationally defined as a heterogeneous solid-appearing area containing multiple small anechoic spaces, was present in 7/13 patients (53.8%), and abundant intralesional vascularity (Adler grade III) was seen in 9/13 patients (69.2%). This microcystic or multicystic appearance may reflect the underlying glandular architecture together with the mucin-containing spaces of gastric-type cervical lesions (4, 6). These findings should, however, be regarded as descriptive imaging clues rather than as specific diagnostic signs.Not all G-EAC lesions showed an overtly malignant sonographic appearance. Although the original preoperative ultrasound reports raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in most of these patients, some were interpreted as benign cervical cystic lesions, whereas others showed no cervical abnormality. This variability highlights an important diagnostic pitfall in ultrasound. Lesions that are predominantly cystic or multicystic may resemble benign cervical conditions, whereas deeply located lesions, and those without marked cervical enlargement, may be difficult to identify on routine sonographic examination. The absence of an obvious solid mass or of other features conventionally regarded as malignant should not preclude consideration of G-EAC when clinical or imaging findings remain suspicious.The mere presence of multiple cervical cystic spaces is by itself insufficient to distinguish G-EAC from benign multicystic cervical lesions. Nabothian cysts and lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia (LEGH) may show overlapping imaging features, and gastric-type neoplastic lesions may themselves show variable proportions of solid and cystic components (12–14). Sonographic morphology should therefore be assessed in the context of lesion margins, solid components, vascularity, clinical presentation, and complementary imaging rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic feature.Color Doppler showed abundant intralesional vascularity in a considerable proportion of patients in this series. This observation likewise warrants cautious interpretation. Adler grading was originally developed as a semiquantitative framework for describing color Doppler vascularity (3) and has not been validated specifically as a diagnostic grading system for cervical G-EAC. Detailed Doppler acquisition parameters were not uniformly retrievable owing to the retrospective design. Adler grade III vascularity in the present series should therefore be regarded as an exploratory sonographic observation rather than a validated diagnostic criterion.A barrel-shaped cervix has been reported in the imaging literature on gastric-type and minimal deviation cervical adenocarcinoma (15–17). In our cohort, a barrel-shaped cervix was documented in only a few patients; these observations, however, came from pathological or surgical records rather than from a standardized prospective sonographic assessment. This finding should not be interpreted as a sonographic detection rate or as a validated sonographic feature in this study.Differential diagnosis and the complementary role of MRI and pathologyDistinguishing G-EAC from benign multicystic cervical lesions is challenging, because both neoplastic and non-neoplastic processes may contain numerous glandular and cystic structures. The relevant differential diagnoses include nabothian cysts, LEGH, minimal deviation adenocarcinoma (MDA), and other cervical adenocarcinomas. MDA is now considered part of the morphological spectrum of gastric-type adenocarcinoma and may show predominantly cystic or multicystic features (6, 15). LEGH, a gastric-type glandular proliferation, may likewise produce multicystic cervical abnormalities that overlap with those seen in gastric-type neoplastic lesions (12–14). Multicystic architecture alone should not be considered diagnostic of malignancy.MRI can provide complementary information by better characterizing both the distribution of the cystic and solid components and the extent of cervical stromal involvement (12, 14, 16, 17). Earlier MRI studies have examined the characteristic patterns of gastric-type mucin-positive cervical lesions and how these differ from other benign multicystic cervical lesions. The “cosmos pattern,” comprising centrally clustered small cystic and solid components with relatively larger peripheral cysts, has been described in the evaluation of gastric-type mucin-positive cervical lesions (14). This pattern is, however, not specific to invasive G-EAC, because it may also be seen in LEGH, and overlap with other benign cervical cystic lesions has been documented (12–14). MRI findings should therefore be interpreted within the wider clinical and pathological context rather than as a stand-alone diagnostic criterion.In clinical practice, ultrasound and MRI are best regarded as complementary rather than competing examinations. Ultrasound offers an accessible first assessment of cervical morphology, internal echogenicity, cystic architecture, and vascularity, whereas MRI may further characterize lesion architecture and local extent. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionGastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma is an HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinoma that may be difficult to detect with conventional cervical screening and that may show heterogeneous sonographic appearances. In this series, a honeycomb-like pattern and abundant intralesional vascularity were frequently observed at ultrasound, whereas other lesions appeared as benign cystic lesions or showed no obvious cervical abnormality. These findings may offer useful imaging clues that raise clinical suspicion, yet they should not be regarded as specific or validated diagnostic criteria. Persistent vaginal discharge or abnormal bleeding, as well as suspicious cervical imaging findings, warrant careful clinical evaluation even when HPV testing, cytology, or superficial biopsy are negative. Integrating the clinical findings, ultrasound and complementary MRI, and adequate histopathological assessment may support earlier recognition of G-EAC. Larger prospective controlled studies will be needed to validate both the diagnostic relevance and the reproducibility of these sonographic findings.

full_text: SUMMARYOBJECTIVE:The aim of this study was to assess how initial loop electrosurgical excision procedure margin subtype, glandular involvement, endocervical curettage findings, and specimen size relate to re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology and receipt of further surgery.METHODS:In this retrospective cohort study, 287 patients undergoing re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure at a tertiary center (2015–2025) were reviewed. Initial margin status was classified as margin continuity, margin adjacency, or non-evaluable margin. Associations with re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology, residual CIN2+ disease, and receipt of a third surgical intervention were assessed using chi-square/Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, Cohen's kappa, and multivariate logistic regression.RESULTS:Initial and re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology showed a significant group-level association (p=0.039) but no case-by-case agreement beyond chance (kappa=-0.009, p=0.754); most patients with initial CIN2/3 had CIN1 at re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure. Margin adjacency independently predicted residual CIN2+ disease at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure (OR 11.045, p=0.049), as did glandular involvement (OR 1.938, p=0.035). Among patients with negative re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure margins, residual CIN2+ disease was identified within the specimen in 27.1%, and human papillomavirus test negativity at the first follow-up visit was 88.2%, varying by genotype. Positive margin (OR 333.33, p<0.001) and positive endocervical curettage (OR 41.67, p<0.001) at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure were the strongest predictors of receiving a third surgical intervention.CONCLUSION:Margin adjacency and glandular involvement independently predicted residual CIN2+ at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure, whereas positive margins and positive endocervical curettage at re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure were strongly associated with receipt of a third surgical intervention. Post-loop electrosurgical excision procedure follow-up should integrate margin subtype, glandular involvement, endocervical curettage findings, and human papillomavirus surveillance rather than rely on margin status alone; genotype-specific differences in human papillomavirus test negativity require confirmation in larger cohorts.KEYWORDS: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, Neoplasm, Surgical margin, Residual disease, Human papillomavirus, Re-excision METHODSStudy design and settingThis retrospective, non-interventional cohort study was conducted at S.B.U. Izmir Tepecik Training and Research Hospital, University of Health Sciences, Izmir, Turkiye, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and was approved by the institution's Non-Interventional Research Ethics Committee (approval no. 2025/12-07, January 5, 2026). Given the retrospective design, individual informed consent was waived.Study populationWe reviewed patients who underwent colposcopy-directed biopsy and subsequent LEEP for histologically confirmed CIN at our center between January 2015 and December 2025, and who underwent a second (re-)LEEP because of a positive or margin-adjacent surgical margin, a positive ECC, an indeterminate margin, or high-grade cytology on follow-up (positive margin in 202 patients, combined positive margin and ECC in 47, indeterminate margin in 31, isolated positive ECC in 5, and atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (ASC-H) cytology in 2). At histopathological classification, these indications corresponded to margin continuity or margin adjacency in 251 patients and to a non-evaluable margin in 36. Patients with a clear negative initial margin, those who declined re-LEEP, those with invasive carcinoma at initial LEEP or biopsy, those who underwent primary hysterectomy without a second excisional procedure, and those with incomplete records were excluded. A minimum interval of 6 weeks was required between the initial LEEP and re-LEEP; after this minimum interval, re-LEEP was scheduled for the earliest possible time after this period.Data collection and variable definitionsDemographic characteristics, baseline HPV genotype and cytology, colposcopy-directed biopsy results, and initial LEEP findings (histopathology, glandular involvement, ECC, margin status, specimen size) were extracted from institutional records. Margin status at initial LEEP was classified as margin continuity (CIN extending continuously to the cut edge), margin adjacency (CIN within 1 mm of the margin without unequivocal transection), or non-evaluable margin (status unassessable, typically due to thermal artifact) 12,13 . full_text_sections.abstract: SUMMARYOBJECTIVE:The aim of this study was to assess how initial loop electrosurgical excision procedure margin subtype, glandular involvement, endocervical curettage findings, and specimen size relate to re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology and receipt of further surgery.METHODS:In this retrospective cohort study, 287 patients undergoing re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure at a tertiary center (2015–2025) were reviewed. Initial margin status was classified as margin continuity, margin adjacency, or non-evaluable margin. Associations with re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology, residual CIN2+ disease, and receipt of a third surgical intervention were assessed using chi-square/Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, Cohen's kappa, and multivariate logistic regression.RESULTS:Initial and re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure pathology showed a significant group-level association (p=0.039) but no case-by-case agreement beyond chance (kappa=-0.009, p=0.754); most patients with initial CIN2/3 had CIN1 at re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure. Margin adjacency independently predicted residual CIN2+ disease at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure (OR 11.045, p=0.049), as did glandular involvement (OR 1.938, p=0.035). Among patients with negative re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure margins, residual CIN2+ disease was identified within the specimen in 27.1%, and human papillomavirus test negativity at the first follow-up visit was 88.2%, varying by genotype. Positive margin (OR 333.33, p<0.001) and positive endocervical curettage (OR 41.67, p<0.001) at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure were the strongest predictors of receiving a third surgical intervention.CONCLUSION:Margin adjacency and glandular involvement independently predicted residual CIN2+ at repeat loop electrosurgical excision procedure, whereas positive margins and positive endocervical curettage at re-loop electrosurgical excision procedure were strongly associated with receipt of a third surgical intervention. Post-loop electrosurgical excision procedure follow-up should integrate margin subtype, glandular involvement, endocervical curettage findings, and human papillomavirus surveillance rather than rely on margin status alone; genotype-specific differences in human papillomavirus test negativity require confirmation in larger cohorts.KEYWORDS: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, Neoplasm, Surgical margin, Residual disease, Human papillomavirus, Re-excision

full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThis study evaluated initial LEEP margin subtype, glandular involvement, and ECC findings as predictors of re-LEEP outcomes and residual disease. Initial and re-LEEP pathology showed a significant group-level association but no case-by-case agreement beyond chance (kappa=-0.009), indicating that initial histopathology did not reliably predict re-LEEP histology at the individual-patient level. This finding is consistent with prior evidence that margin status alone has limited sensitivity for residual or recurrent CIN2+ compared with post-treatment HPV testing 7 . However, the observed discordance should not be interpreted as evidence of a distinct disease process, because the predominance of CIN1 at re-LEEP may simply reflect removal of the bulk of the high-grade lesion during the initial excision. Fernández-Montolí et al. similarly found that HR-HPV positivity and margin involvement independently predicted residual or recurrent CIN2-3 despite limited histopathological concordance 11 , and HPV persistence was the only consistent predictor of recurrence across excision techniques in a 5-year follow-up study 14 . These findings support integrating markers beyond simple pathology concordance into clinical decision-making.Margin adjacency was the category most closely linked to high-grade residual disease and remained an independent predictor after adjustment (OR 11.045, p=0.049), consistent with Fernández-Montolí et al.'s finding that uncertain margins carried the highest recurrence risk (OR 15.84) 11 and with Abdulaziz et al.'s report that multifocal margin involvement increased residual disease risk 15 . In contrast, Bruno et al. found cone margin status was not an independent predictor in a postmenopausal CIN3 population 16 , a discrepancy likely reflecting differences in age distribution and margin categorization. Specimen size did not differ across margin categories in our cohort, partly contrasting with Ge et al.'s finding that cone depth >0.5 cm was protective against recurrence 17 , and with Kim et al.'s observation that cone depth and margin involvement varied by whether glandular involvement was recognized before conization 9 .Glandular involvement has previously been linked to more aggressive management without clearly worse outcomes; Kim et al. found that glandular involvement-positive patients underwent additional procedures more often despite similar residual or recurrence rates 9 , and Paternostro et al. questioned the value of routine ECC, which altered management in only 1.7% of cases and had a negative predictive value of 43.8% 18 . In our cohort, glandular involvement was not associated with ECC findings or margin status but independently predicted residual CIN2+ at repeat LEEP (OR 1.938, p=0.035). ECC positivity has also been reported as the second strongest independent predictor of residual disease after HPV persistence in postmenopausal patients 16 . In our dataset, however, initial ECC was not independently associated with residual CIN2+, whereas positive ECC at re-LEEP was strongly associated with receipt of a third surgical intervention; these findings represent different procedural stages and endpoints and should not be interpreted as a single prognostic effect. These findings extend our previous work, in which HPV subtype was not independently associated with the rate of positive surgical margin after cervical conization 19 , and endocervical glandular involvement did not differ significantly by cone specimen depth 20 .For receipt of a third intervention, positive margin (OR 333.33) and positive ECC (OR 41.67) at re-LEEP were the strongest predictors, in line with Arbyn et al.'s report of an approximately five-fold increase in treatment failure with positive margins 7 and Reimers et al.'s finding of a strong association between positive margins and recurrence in human immunodeficiency virus-positive women 21 . That margin and ECC status at the second LEEP were more predictive than initial findings suggests a cumulative effect of risk factors across successive interventions. This finding has practical implications: post-re-LEEP surveillance may warrant closer attention than post-initial-LEEP surveillance, since risk appears to compound rather than reset with each subsequent procedure.Negative re-LEEP margins did not guarantee HPV test negativity at the first follow-up visit, although negativity reached 88.2% overall and was highest for HPV16 (91.3%) and lowest for HPV18 and multiple infections. This is consistent with Lin et al.'s meta-analysis reporting a 22.7% residual HPV rate after LEEP with negative margins and a 3.6-fold increase in CIN recurrence risk with residual HPV 22 , and with Heydari et al.'s finding that negative HR-HPV combined with clear margins yielded a 98.7% negative predictive value, whereas clear margins alone did not 23 . Persistent HPV positivity has also emerged as the strongest independent predictor of residual disease in postmenopausal CIN3 populations 16 , reinforcing that margin status alone is insufficient; the trend toward genotype-specific differences in HPV test negativity observed here (p=0.099) did not reach significance and would require confirmation in larger cohorts before informing surveillance strategy. Adjunctive molecular strategies may help address this gap: combining HPV testing with p16/Ki-67 dual staining, even on self-sampled material, has been shown to accurately identify women at risk for cervical cancer 24 , suggesting a possible complementary approach to margin- and genotype-based surveillance alone.Taken together, margin adjacency and glandular involvement at initial LEEP independently predicted residual CIN2+ at re-LEEP, whereas positive margin and positive ECC at re-LEEP were strongly associated with receipt of a third surgical intervention. As a preliminary, hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated clinical guideline, these stage-specific findings may help structure post-re-LEEP surveillance; prospective validation in an independent cohort is required before clinical adoption.Strengths of this study include the systematic evaluation of pathological and virological data across two procedures, the analysis of margin subtypes as distinct categories, and separate examination of patients receiving a third intervention, offering more detailed risk stratification than studies limited to binary margin classification. A further strength is the explicit separation of margin adjacency from both frank margin continuity and non-evaluable margins, a distinction blurred in much of the prior literature. Limitations include the retrospective, single-center design, non-standardized repeat HPV genotyping, and short follow-up, which was particularly limiting for assessing HPV clearance and recurrence. The margin adjacency subgroup was small, with a wide confidence interval (OR 11.045, 95%CI 1.015–120.181); pooling it with margin continuity abolished the significant association (OR 0.68, 95%CI 0.30–1.52, p=0.34), indicating the two behave differently, so we retained margin adjacency as a distinct category. Receipt of a third intervention was itself informed by re-LEEP margin and ECC findings, introducing incorporation bias that likely contributes to the very high odds ratios observed for these predictors (OR 333.33 and 41.67); together with the small event numbers and high Nagelkerke R-squared (0.77), these results should be read as exploratory rather than confirmatory, and comparisons were not corrected for multiple testing. Prospective, multicenter validation of the margin subtype classification would help confirm its clinical utility.
full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONMargin subtypes at initial LEEP, particularly margin adjacency, carry significant but case-wise limited value in predicting residual high-grade disease at re-LEEP. Glandular involvement at initial LEEP independently predicted residual CIN2+, whereas positive margin and positive ECC at re-LEEP were strongly associated with receipt of a third surgical intervention. Post-LEEP follow-up should therefore adopt a risk-based approach integrating HPV testing and stage-specific histopathological findings rather than relying on margin status alone; the incremental value of genotype-specific surveillance remains to be established.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONCervical cancer remains one of the most common gynecological malignancies worldwide, and nearly every case traces back to persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, with genotypes 16 and 18 predominating 1,2 . Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is the histological precursor spectrum, ranging from low-grade lesions prone to spontaneous regression to high-grade lesions (CIN2/3) that carry a meaningful risk of progression to invasive carcinoma if untreated 3,4 . Although active surveillance is increasingly used for selected young women with CIN2, CIN3 and persistent or progressive CIN2 still warrant excisional treatment 5 .Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) is the most widely used excisional technique for high-grade CIN, given its favorable safety profile, low cost, and ability to provide a specimen for margin assessment 6 . Despite this, a substantial proportion of patients have disease at or near the excision margin, and margin status remains one of the strongest predictors of treatment failure, with meta-analytic data showing markedly higher recurrence risk with positive versus negative margins 7 . This creates a clinical dilemma. Repeat excision or hysterectomy is often considered for positive margins, yet many such patients do not, in fact, harbor residual disease, raising concerns about overtreatment given the known association between excisional treatment and adverse obstetric outcomes such as preterm birth 8 .Beyond binary margin status, features such as the extent of margin involvement, glandular involvement, ECC findings, and specimen size have been proposed as additional prognostic markers 9,10 . However, most literature still relies on binary margin classification, and little is known about how more granular categories, margin adjacency without transection, margin continuity, and non-evaluable margins due to thermal artifact, relate to outcomes at repeat excision 7,11 . Data are also limited on patients requiring a third surgical intervention and on genotype-specific HPV clearance after negative re-LEEP margins.We therefore conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing re-LEEP at a tertiary referral center over an 11-year period, evaluating whether findings at repeat excision can be anticipated from the initial specimen at all, and how detailed initial margin subtypes, glandular involvement, ECC findings, and specimen characteristics relate to re-LEEP pathology and receipt of further surgery, to identify which initial histopathological features most reliably predict clinically meaningful residual disease. Study populationWe reviewed patients who underwent colposcopy-directed biopsy and subsequent LEEP for histologically confirmed CIN at our center between January 2015 and December 2025, and who underwent a second (re-)LEEP because of a positive or margin-adjacent surgical margin, a positive ECC, an indeterminate margin, or high-grade cytology on follow-up (positive margin in 202 patients, combined positive margin and ECC in 47, indeterminate margin in 31, isolated positive ECC in 5, and atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (ASC-H) cytology in 2). At histopathological classification, these indications corresponded to margin continuity or margin adjacency in 251 patients and to a non-evaluable margin in 36. Patients with a clear negative initial margin, those who declined re-LEEP, those with invasive carcinoma at initial LEEP or biopsy, those who underwent primary hysterectomy without a second excisional procedure, and those with incomplete records were excluded. A minimum interval of 6 weeks was required between the initial LEEP and re-LEEP; after this minimum interval, re-LEEP was scheduled for the earliest possible time after this period. Data collection and variable definitionsDemographic characteristics, baseline HPV genotype and cytology, colposcopy-directed biopsy results, and initial LEEP findings (histopathology, glandular involvement, ECC, margin status, specimen size) were extracted from institutional records. Margin status at initial LEEP was classified as margin continuity (CIN extending continuously to the cut edge), margin adjacency (CIN within 1 mm of the margin without unequivocal transection), or non-evaluable margin (status unassessable, typically due to thermal artifact) 12,13 . Margin status was assigned from the routine histopathological report generated at the original procedure rather than by re-review of specimens for this study; when thermal artifact was present but the reporting pathologist was nonetheless able to render a margin call, that call determined classification as continuity or adjacency, and only specimens for which no margin call could be made were classified as non-evaluable. Margin distance was assessed visually by the reporting pathologist under routine light microscopy; a standardized micrometer-based measurement protocol was not used, and inter-observer variability in this assessment was not formally evaluated. Findings at re-LEEP included histopathology, glandular involvement, ECC, and margin status; patients were further stratified by whether a third intervention (repeat LEEP, cold-knife conization, or hysterectomy) was performed. ECC was routinely performed after the excisional procedure. Positive ECC was defined as CIN2 or worse on endocervical curettage. ECC performed immediately after LEEP carries a theoretical risk of contamination by excision-related blood or tissue, which could affect interpretation; this reflects standard clinical practice, and specimens were interpreted by experienced gynecologic pathologists. Follow-up HPV testing and cytology were performed at the first post-re-LEEP visit. HPV clearance was defined as a negative test at this visit and persistence as a positive test; because sequential genotype-level comparison was not performed, true persistence of the original genotype could not be distinguished from reinfection with a new genotype. Statistical analysisContinuous variables were expressed as median (interquartile range [IQR]) or mean +/- SD and compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test; categorical variables were compared using the chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test, with linear-by-linear association tests for ordered categories. Agreement between initial and re-LEEP pathology was assessed with Cohen's kappa. Multivariate logistic regression identified independent predictors of residual CIN2+ disease and receipt of a third surgical intervention, with model fit assessed by the Hosmer-Lemeshow test and Nagelkerke R-squared. Two-sided p<0.05 was considered significant. Analyses used SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). full_text: AbstractFemale reproductive diseases (FRDs) substantially affect women’s health and fertility, with lipid metabolic reprogramming emerging as a shared pathological feature. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSLs) activate long-chain fatty acids and direct lipid flux toward β-oxidation, lipid synthesis, and phospholipid remodeling, thereby influencing oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and inflammatory signaling. Unlike previous reviews centered on broad ACSL biology, selected isoforms, or pathway-based ferroptosis mechanisms, this review adopts a disease-spanning, isoform-specific framework. We compare ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL4, ACSL5, and ACSL6 across cervical, ovarian, and endometrial cancers, polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, and preeclampsia. By integrating isoform-specific substrate preference, subcellular localization, and lipid-channeling functions, we examine how individual ACSLs differentially regulate fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis and phospholipid remodeling, ferroptosis sensitivity, and inflammatory signaling across reproductive disease contexts. We further distinguish disease-specific experimental evidence from bioinformatic associations and mechanistic extrapolations from other disease models. Current evidence most consistently supports a disease-relevant role for ACSL4 in ferroptosis regulation, whereas ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL5, and ACSL6 show greater context dependence. This integrated framework identifies shared metabolic mechanisms, disease-specific differences, and priorities for cell-resolved validation and future isoform-selective therapeutic development.Keywords: female reproductive diseases, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase, lipid metabolic reprogramming, ferroptosis, inflammatory signaling. 8.Discussion and future perspectivesAcross female reproductive diseases (FRDs), ACSL isoforms are best understood as context-dependent metabolic gatekeepers rather than uniformly pro- or anti-disease factors. Their biological effects depend on fatty-acid substrate preference, subcellular localization, cell type, and the metabolic pathway into which activated fatty acids are channeled (30, 31). ACSL4 illustrates this context dependence particularly clearly. In cervical cancer, ACSL4-dependent ferroptosis can suppress tumor growth and metastatic behavior (62), whereas in ovarian cancer, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-lipid synthesis can promote metastatic extravasation and colonization while simultaneously creating increased ferroptosis susceptibility (43). In non-neoplastic reproductive disorders, ACSL4-associated lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic phenotypes have been linked to impaired endometrial function in endometriosis (45, 97) and trophoblast dysfunction in preeclampsia (121, 122). These apparently divergent effects emphasize that the pathological consequences of ACSL4 activity cannot be inferred from isoform identity alone but must be interpreted according to disease and cellular context.The strength of evidence also differs substantially among ACSL isoforms. ACSL4 currently has the broadest disease-specific functional support across the reproductive conditions reviewed, although the direction and mechanism of its effects remain disease- and cell-context dependent. ACSL1 has direct functional evidence in selected settings, particularly ovarian and endometrial cancer, but its roles cannot yet be generalized across FRDs. By contrast, many proposed functions of ACSL3 and ACSL5 remain based on transcriptomic associations, pathway-level observations, or mechanistic extrapolation from non-reproductive models, while ACSL6 remains poorly characterized in most reproductive diseases. Similarly, increases in ROS, MDA, Fe2+, or changes in GPX4 alone should be regarded as ferroptosis-associated evidence rather than definitive proof of ferroptotic cell death; stronger conclusions require ferroptosis-specific functional validation, ideally including rescue experiments and complementary genetic or mechanistic evidence. Table 2 summarizes the supporting evidence, while Figure 8 provides an overview of isoform-specific involvement and associated pathways across FRDs.Figure 8Isoform-specific involvement of ACSLs in female reproductive diseases. The circular diagram summarizes the associations between ACSL isoforms and disease-related pathways in female reproductive diseases. The center represents ACSLs, the inner sectors indicate disease categories, and the outer segments show specific ACSL isoforms and their associated mechanisms. These mechanisms include lipid reprogramming, ferroptosis, fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis, apoptosis, metastasis, insulin resistance, trophoblast dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and impaired endometrial receptivity. ACSL, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase; FRDs, female reproductive diseases; HPV, human papillomavirus; SCD, stearoyl-CoA desaturase; PUFA, polyunsaturated fatty acid; MUFA, monounsaturated fatty acid; FASN, fatty acid synthase; LPO, lipid peroxidation; FAO, fatty acid oxidation; CPT1C, carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1C; SOD1, superoxide dismutase 1; GTF2E2, general transcription factor IIE subunit 2; AMPK, AMP-activated protein kinase; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase; Akt, protein kinase B; mTOR, mechanistic target of rapamycin; DHT, dihydrotestosterone; ATF4, activating transcription factor 4; MMP2/9, matrix metalloproteinase 2/9; METTL3, methyltransferase-like 3; m6A, N6-methyladenosine; ELF5, E74-like ETS transcription factor 5; p53, tumor protein p53.Circular infographic shows relationships between ACSL family members (ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL4, ACSL5, ACSL6) and their roles in conditions such as cervical cancer, preeclampsia, endometrial cancer, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, and polycystic ovary syndrome, including detailed pathways and molecular effects for each condition.Future studies should therefore prioritize causal, cell-type-resolved validation rather than further expansion of associative gene signatures. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches can identify the cellular sources of individual ACSL isoforms, whereas targeted lipidomics and stable-isotope tracing can determine how each isoform redirects fatty-acid flux into oxidation, storage, or oxidation-prone membrane phospholipids. These approaches should be combined with isoform-specific genetic perturbation in primary cells, patient-derived organoids, trophoblast models, and appropriate in vivo systems. Such integrated experiments will be particularly important for separating ACSL-dependent lipid remodeling from downstream ferroptosis-associated marker changes and for determining whether the same isoform exerts distinct effects across tumor, ovarian, endometrial, and placental cell populations.Translation of ACSL biology into therapy also faces important pharmacological limitations. Selective pharmacological tools remain limited and are not broadly available across ACSL isoforms, although potent selective inhibitors have been developed for ACSL1 and, more recently, ACSL4 (124, 125). Earlier ACSL4-directed compounds also illustrate the importance of carefully evaluating target selectivity and off-target pharmacology; for example, rosiglitazone has ACSL4-inhibitory activity but also acts on PPARγ, whereas newer compounds have been developed to improve ACSL4 selectivity (125). Because ACSLs participate in physiological fatty-acid activation and channeling into distinct metabolic pathways (30), systemic inhibition may perturb normal lipid homeostasis outside the diseased tissue. Future therapeutic development should therefore emphasize isoform selectivity, tissue- or cell-targeted delivery, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers that confirm on-target lipid remodeling. These requirements are especially important in non-malignant reproductive disorders and pregnancy. Thus, the immediate priority is not broad clinical inhibition of the ACSL family, but rigorous validation of disease-specific ACSL dependencies followed by development of selective and context-appropriate intervention strategies. 9.ConclusionIn conclusion, ACSL isoforms provide an isoform- and context-specific link between lipid metabolic reprogramming, phospholipid remodeling, ferroptosis susceptibility, and inflammatory signaling in female reproductive diseases. Among the family members reviewed, ACSL4 currently has the strongest and most reproducible disease-specific functional evidence across multiple reproductive disorders, although its biological consequences differ among malignant and non-malignant tissues. ACSL1 has direct functional support in selected disease contexts, whereas ACSL3, ACSL5, and ACSL6 remain predominantly candidate metabolic nodes supported by more limited, associative, or extrapolated evidence. These knowledge gaps, together with the limited availability of isoform-selective pharmacological tools, currently preclude immediate clinical translation of most ACSL-directed strategies. Future progress will depend on cell-type-resolved functional studies, rigorous ferroptosis-specific validation, and the development of selective, tissue-appropriate approaches for modulating individual ACSL isoforms. 1.IntroductionThe health of the female reproductive system profoundly impacts individual quality of life and sustainable population development (1). However, a series of complex female reproductive diseases (FRDs) severely affect the physiological functions, psychological states, and fertility of hundreds of millions of women worldwide, constituting a major public health challenge. These disorders often exhibit multifactorial etiologies, intertwined mechanisms, and clinical heterogeneity, with strong interrelationships that complicate diagnosis and treatment. Despite differences in clinical manifestations and target organs among various FRDs, growing evidence suggests they may share core pathological mechanisms, such as lipid metabolism reprogramming, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and cellular energy metabolism (2). Among these, lipid metabolism abnormalities have increasingly been identified as a key common pathway. Lipid metabolic reprogramming contributes to disease onset and progression through multiple mechanisms, including regulation of cellular signaling, membrane stability, and inflammatory responses (3). Therefore, re-examining FRDs from a metabolic perspective—particularly by focusing on key regulatory molecules in lipid metabolism such as the ACSLs—holds promise for revealing their common pathogenic mechanisms and developing novel intervention strategies.Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSLs) regulate physiological and pathological processes in the female reproductive system by modulating fatty acid activation, lipid synthesis, and lipid signaling pathways (4). Unlike short- and medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, ACSLs preferentially activate long-chain fatty acids, typically containing 12–20 carbon atoms, to form fatty acyl-CoAs, thereby supporting fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis, and membrane remodeling. Among ACSL isoforms, ACSL4 provides a particularly relevant link between lipid activation and hormone-dependent biology. Early functional studies demonstrated that suppression of ACSL4 impairs hormone-stimulated steroidogenesis, supporting a role for ACSL4-dependent arachidonic acid metabolism in steroidogenic signaling and StAR-associated cholesterol transport (5). Subsequent studies further linked ACSL4 dysregulation to enhanced proliferation, migration, invasion, and therapeutic resistance in hormone-responsive and hormone-refractory tumor models (6). Extensive research indicates that abnormal ACSL expression and function are closely associated with lipid metabolism reprogramming in various FRDs, including endometrial cancer (EC) and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) (7–9). Therefore, this review aims to systematically examine the isoform-specific roles and regulatory mechanisms of ACSLs across FRDs, thereby clarifying their shared and disease-specific metabolic mechanisms and identifying priorities for future mechanistic and translational studies. ACSLs catalyze the ATP-dependent two-step activation of long-chain fatty acids at membrane-associated sites, including the endoplasmic reticulum and the outer mitochondrial membrane, generating long-chain acyl-CoAs that can subsequently enter fatty acid oxidation (FAO) or lipid biosynthetic pathways (10). In mammals, although ACSLs share overlapping catalytic functions, they exhibit distinct patterns of tissue distribution, subcellular localization, and substrate preference (11)(Table 1). Such specificity suggests that each ACSL isoform is precisely positioned to channel fatty acids into specific metabolic pathways, thereby acting as a “gatekeeper” of lipid flux. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulation of ACSL expression and activity is closely associated with a spectrum of metabolic disorders, including hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance, atherosclerosis, neurological diseases, and certain types of cancer (14), establishing ACSLs as central regulators of cellular energy homeostasis and lipid signaling.Table 1Characteristics of the ACSLs.ACSLSubcellular distributionFunctionTissue expression(From High to Low)Chromosome localizationSize (number of amino acids)Molecular mass(Da)ACSL1Outer mitochondrial membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, peroxisomal membrane, cytoplasmic lipid dropletMitochondrial β-oxidation: Occurs at the mitochondrial outer membrane, supplies substrates for CPT1.Peroxisomal β-oxidation: Provides substrates for this process.Involved in triglyceride synthesis in the liver and adipose tissue.Heart, skeletal muscle, brown adipose tissue, white adipose tissue, liver, and kidney – expressed most abundantly in tissues with high energy demands.4q35.169877,943ACSL3Endoplasmic reticulum, cytoplasmic lipid droplet, nuclear envelopeLipid droplet formation: Highly enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum and nascent lipid droplets.Membrane phospholipid synthesis: Provides acyl-CoA substrates for phosphatidic acid synthesis.Signal transduction: May participate in nuclear signaling regulation through the generation of acyl-CoA.Liver, lung, brain, mammary gland, adrenal gland, and prostate — expressed at higher levels in tissues with active lipid synthesis.2q36.172080,420ACSL4Endoplasmic reticulum (ER), including mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAMs); ACSL isoforms show distinct intracellular localizations and tissue expression profiles, suggesting that different ACSL members may participate in lipid metabolism through isoform-specific mechanisms.In recent years, ACSLs have been recognized not only for their metabolic roles but also for directly regulating cellular signaling and fate. This functional expansion centers on fatty acyl-CoAs, which act as both a metabolic intermediate and a signaling/modification substrate. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by the accumulation of lipid peroxides in cellular membranes (15). ACSL-mediated fatty acid activation and phospholipid remodeling can influence ferroptosis sensitivity by determining the availability of oxidizable lipid substrates. In particular, ACSL4 preferentially activates PUFAs, especially AA and AdA, facilitating their incorporation into membrane phospholipids and thereby increasing susceptibility to lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis (16, 17). This lipid-remodeling function renders ACSL4 a major determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity, as established by Doll et al. (17). ACSL-mediated lipid remodeling also intersects with inflammatory signaling. ACSL4-dependent AA metabolism can influence the availability of substrates for eicosanoid synthesis, including prostaglandins and leukotrienes, thereby providing a biochemical link between lipid metabolism, ferroptosis, and inflammatory signaling (18). In addition, specific ACSL isoforms, such as ACSL1 and ACSL3, have been implicated in the regulation of gene expression and stress responses through enzyme activity-independent functions, acting as signaling scaffolds or transcriptional regulators (19). Therefore, ACSLs can be considered core molecular nodes linking cellular metabolic states with a broad range of biological processes, including cell death, signal transduction, and gene expression, and their dysregulation may be closely associated with multiple ferroptosis-related diseases. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractFemale reproductive diseases (FRDs) substantially affect women’s health and fertility, with lipid metabolic reprogramming emerging as a shared pathological feature. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSLs) activate long-chain fatty acids and direct lipid flux toward β-oxidation, lipid synthesis, and phospholipid remodeling, thereby influencing oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and inflammatory signaling. Unlike previous reviews centered on broad ACSL biology, selected isoforms, or pathway-based ferroptosis mechanisms, this review adopts a disease-spanning, isoform-specific framework. We compare ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL4, ACSL5, and ACSL6 across cervical, ovarian, and endometrial cancers, polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, and preeclampsia. By integrating isoform-specific substrate preference, subcellular localization, and lipid-channeling functions, we examine how individual ACSLs differentially regulate fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis and phospholipid remodeling, ferroptosis sensitivity, and inflammatory signaling across reproductive disease contexts. We further distinguish disease-specific experimental evidence from bioinformatic associations and mechanistic extrapolations from other disease models. Current evidence most consistently supports a disease-relevant role for ACSL4 in ferroptosis regulation, whereas ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL5, and ACSL6 show greater context dependence. This integrated framework identifies shared metabolic mechanisms, disease-specific differences, and priorities for cell-resolved validation and future isoform-selective therapeutic development.Keywords: female reproductive diseases, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase, lipid metabolic reprogramming, ferroptosis, inflammatory signaling.
full_text_sections.discussion: 8.Discussion and future perspectivesAcross female reproductive diseases (FRDs), ACSL isoforms are best understood as context-dependent metabolic gatekeepers rather than uniformly pro- or anti-disease factors. Their biological effects depend on fatty-acid substrate preference, subcellular localization, cell type, and the metabolic pathway into which activated fatty acids are channeled (30, 31). ACSL4 illustrates this context dependence particularly clearly. In cervical cancer, ACSL4-dependent ferroptosis can suppress tumor growth and metastatic behavior (62), whereas in ovarian cancer, ACSL4-dependent PUFA-lipid synthesis can promote metastatic extravasation and colonization while simultaneously creating increased ferroptosis susceptibility (43). In non-neoplastic reproductive disorders, ACSL4-associated lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic phenotypes have been linked to impaired endometrial function in endometriosis (45, 97) and trophoblast dysfunction in preeclampsia (121, 122). These apparently divergent effects emphasize that the pathological consequences of ACSL4 activity cannot be inferred from isoform identity alone but must be interpreted according to disease and cellular context.The strength of evidence also differs substantially among ACSL isoforms. ACSL4 currently has the broadest disease-specific functional support across the reproductive conditions reviewed, although the direction and mechanism of its effects remain disease- and cell-context dependent. ACSL1 has direct functional evidence in selected settings, particularly ovarian and endometrial cancer, but its roles cannot yet be generalized across FRDs. By contrast, many proposed functions of ACSL3 and ACSL5 remain based on transcriptomic associations, pathway-level observations, or mechanistic extrapolation from non-reproductive models, while ACSL6 remains poorly characterized in most reproductive diseases. Similarly, increases in ROS, MDA, Fe2+, or changes in GPX4 alone should be regarded as ferroptosis-associated evidence rather than definitive proof of ferroptotic cell death; stronger conclusions require ferroptosis-specific functional validation, ideally including rescue experiments and complementary genetic or mechanistic evidence. Table 2 summarizes the supporting evidence, while Figure 8 provides an overview of isoform-specific involvement and associated pathways across FRDs.Figure 8Isoform-specific involvement of ACSLs in female reproductive diseases. The circular diagram summarizes the associations between ACSL isoforms and disease-related pathways in female reproductive diseases. The center represents ACSLs, the inner sectors indicate disease categories, and the outer segments show specific ACSL isoforms and their associated mechanisms. These mechanisms include lipid reprogramming, ferroptosis, fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis, apoptosis, metastasis, insulin resistance, trophoblast dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and impaired endometrial receptivity. ACSL, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase; FRDs, female reproductive diseases; HPV, human papillomavirus; SCD, stearoyl-CoA desaturase; PUFA, polyunsaturated fatty acid; MUFA, monounsaturated fatty acid; FASN, fatty acid synthase; LPO, lipid peroxidation; FAO, fatty acid oxidation; CPT1C, carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1C; SOD1, superoxide dismutase 1; GTF2E2, general transcription factor IIE subunit 2; AMPK, AMP-activated protein kinase; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase; Akt, protein kinase B; mTOR, mechanistic target of rapamycin; DHT, dihydrotestosterone; ATF4, activating transcription factor 4; MMP2/9, matrix metalloproteinase 2/9; METTL3, methyltransferase-like 3; m6A, N6-methyladenosine; ELF5, E74-like ETS transcription factor 5; p53, tumor protein p53.Circular infographic shows relationships between ACSL family members (ACSL1, ACSL3, ACSL4, ACSL5, ACSL6) and their roles in conditions such as cervical cancer, preeclampsia, endometrial cancer, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, and polycystic ovary syndrome, including detailed pathways and molecular effects for each condition.Future studies should therefore prioritize causal, cell-type-resolved validation rather than further expansion of associative gene signatures. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches can identify the cellular sources of individual ACSL isoforms, whereas targeted lipidomics and stable-isotope tracing can determine how each isoform redirects fatty-acid flux into oxidation, storage, or oxidation-prone membrane phospholipids. These approaches should be combined with isoform-specific genetic perturbation in primary cells, patient-derived organoids, trophoblast models, and appropriate in vivo systems. Such integrated experiments will be particularly important for separating ACSL-dependent lipid remodeling from downstream ferroptosis-associated marker changes and for determining whether the same isoform exerts distinct effects across tumor, ovarian, endometrial, and placental cell populations.Translation of ACSL biology into therapy also faces important pharmacological limitations. Selective pharmacological tools remain limited and are not broadly available across ACSL isoforms, although potent selective inhibitors have been developed for ACSL1 and, more recently, ACSL4 (124, 125). Earlier ACSL4-directed compounds also illustrate the importance of carefully evaluating target selectivity and off-target pharmacology; for example, rosiglitazone has ACSL4-inhibitory activity but also acts on PPARγ, whereas newer compounds have been developed to improve ACSL4 selectivity (125). Because ACSLs participate in physiological fatty-acid activation and channeling into distinct metabolic pathways (30), systemic inhibition may perturb normal lipid homeostasis outside the diseased tissue. Future therapeutic development should therefore emphasize isoform selectivity, tissue- or cell-targeted delivery, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers that confirm on-target lipid remodeling. These requirements are especially important in non-malignant reproductive disorders and pregnancy. Thus, the immediate priority is not broad clinical inhibition of the ACSL family, but rigorous validation of disease-specific ACSL dependencies followed by development of selective and context-appropriate intervention strategies.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 9.ConclusionIn conclusion, ACSL isoforms provide an isoform- and context-specific link between lipid metabolic reprogramming, phospholipid remodeling, ferroptosis susceptibility, and inflammatory signaling in female reproductive diseases. Among the family members reviewed, ACSL4 currently has the strongest and most reproducible disease-specific functional evidence across multiple reproductive disorders, although its biological consequences differ among malignant and non-malignant tissues. ACSL1 has direct functional support in selected disease contexts, whereas ACSL3, ACSL5, and ACSL6 remain predominantly candidate metabolic nodes supported by more limited, associative, or extrapolated evidence. These knowledge gaps, together with the limited availability of isoform-selective pharmacological tools, currently preclude immediate clinical translation of most ACSL-directed strategies. Future progress will depend on cell-type-resolved functional studies, rigorous ferroptosis-specific validation, and the development of selective, tissue-appropriate approaches for modulating individual ACSL isoforms.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionThe health of the female reproductive system profoundly impacts individual quality of life and sustainable population development (1). However, a series of complex female reproductive diseases (FRDs) severely affect the physiological functions, psychological states, and fertility of hundreds of millions of women worldwide, constituting a major public health challenge. These disorders often exhibit multifactorial etiologies, intertwined mechanisms, and clinical heterogeneity, with strong interrelationships that complicate diagnosis and treatment. Despite differences in clinical manifestations and target organs among various FRDs, growing evidence suggests they may share core pathological mechanisms, such as lipid metabolism reprogramming, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and cellular energy metabolism (2). Among these, lipid metabolism abnormalities have increasingly been identified as a key common pathway. Lipid metabolic reprogramming contributes to disease onset and progression through multiple mechanisms, including regulation of cellular signaling, membrane stability, and inflammatory responses (3). Therefore, re-examining FRDs from a metabolic perspective—particularly by focusing on key regulatory molecules in lipid metabolism such as the ACSLs—holds promise for revealing their common pathogenic mechanisms and developing novel intervention strategies.Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSLs) regulate physiological and pathological processes in the female reproductive system by modulating fatty acid activation, lipid synthesis, and lipid signaling pathways (4). Unlike short- and medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, ACSLs preferentially activate long-chain fatty acids, typically containing 12–20 carbon atoms, to form fatty acyl-CoAs, thereby supporting fatty acid oxidation, lipid synthesis, and membrane remodeling. Among ACSL isoforms, ACSL4 provides a particularly relevant link between lipid activation and hormone-dependent biology. Early functional studies demonstrated that suppression of ACSL4 impairs hormone-stimulated steroidogenesis, supporting a role for ACSL4-dependent arachidonic acid metabolism in steroidogenic signaling and StAR-associated cholesterol transport (5). Subsequent studies further linked ACSL4 dysregulation to enhanced proliferation, migration, invasion, and therapeutic resistance in hormone-responsive and hormone-refractory tumor models (6). Extensive research indicates that abnormal ACSL expression and function are closely associated with lipid metabolism reprogramming in various FRDs, including endometrial cancer (EC) and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) (7–9). Therefore, this review aims to systematically examine the isoform-specific roles and regulatory mechanisms of ACSLs across FRDs, thereby clarifying their shared and disease-specific metabolic mechanisms and identifying priorities for future mechanistic and translational studies. ACSLs catalyze the ATP-dependent two-step activation of long-chain fatty acids at membrane-associated sites, including the endoplasmic reticulum and the outer mitochondrial membrane, generating long-chain acyl-CoAs that can subsequently enter fatty acid oxidation (FAO) or lipid biosynthetic pathways (10). Such specificity suggests that each ACSL isoform is precisely positioned to channel fatty acids into specific metabolic pathways, thereby acting as a “gatekeeper” of lipid flux.
