full_text: The Expanded Program on Immunization, introduced in 1974, marks a pivotal milestone in public health and celebrates its 50th anniversary in 2024. Originally targeting childhood immunization, the program has expanded to include adolescents and adults, driven by the evolving epidemiology of vaccine-preventable diseases and age-related immunosenescence. The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the vulnerabilities of older populations, reinforcing the need for a lifecourse approach (LCA) to immunization. The article explores the integration of LCA into global health systems, focusing on low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) and India. The article discusses the critical factors and policy-level efforts that India and countries with similar contexts need to consider in expanding immunization programs across the lifecourse. 4DiscussionIntegrating the LCI into existing health systems requires a holistic strategy that emphasizes multi-sectoral coordination and system-wide adaptability to address the evolving health needs of individuals across all stages of life. This requires a strong political commitment to positioning LCA as a part of the national-level strategy. National health authorities and health ministries must clearly articulate LCA’s benefits in health policies and align its goals with the broader SDGs. NITAGs have been pivotal in shaping immunization programs and introducing vaccines for various age groups. As of 2021, more than 80% of countries have established NITAGs, and 69% (119 of 172) meet the six process indicators of WHO to be categorized as functional; IA 2030 has also emphasized the need to strengthen their influence (60, 61). These expert groups provide essential guidance for integrating LCA into immunization programs, helping to prioritize vaccines and develop age-appropriate schedules. Life course immunization emerged as an important focus area and opportunity in the 15th and 18th NITAG-India, held in 2020 and 2023, respectively (62, 63). The absence of age-specific data on VPDs in the Indian population limits efforts to assess and address disease burdens across life stages accurately. While pediatric immunization is adequately covered, adult and older adults cohorts remain underrepresented. This gap disproportionately affects immunocompromised populations, heightening their vulnerability to infections. Without surveillance and resource allocation, adult immunization programs remain fragmented. Strengthening data collection is essential to reduce VPDs and ensure data-driven decision-making for lifecourse immunization.Comprehensive Primary Healthcare (CPHC), an approach to achieving universal health coverage, can be leveraged to expand immunization services. This can be achieved by integrating vaccines into the CPHC framework by aligning vaccination schedules with other routine health services such as maternal and child health visits, school health programs, and geriatric care for older adults. This integration promotes a seamless transition between different life stages, ensuring that vaccination remains a continuous priority throughout a person’s life. One way to achieve this integration is to leverage existing systems, such as electronic health records (EHRs) and immunization registries, to track vaccination status throughout a person’s lifetime. These systems can be linked with other health services, such as screenings and chronic disease management, to ensure that vaccination is part of a broader preventive health strategy. For instance, when an adult visits a clinic for a routine health check-up, their vaccination status can be reviewed, and any missing vaccines recommended for adults can be administered with consent, reinforcing the importance of immunization at every stage of life. Vaccination coverage in the second year of life is often lower than in the first year. Implementation challenges are observed in the second year of life owing to the sub-optimal orientation of the frontline workers to new targets and delivery modes–this also applies to adolescent vaccination (64). In 2024, India launched UWIN, a name-based digital registry system to enhance the immunization program through efficient tracking and real-time monitoring. The platform also offers a self-registration feature for all eligible citizens. UWIN is inspired by the success of COWIN, a platform that boosted vaccination rates among adults and the older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. This technological integration will pave the way for future lifecourse vaccines in the country (65, 66).Multi-sectoral stakeholder engagement requires attention owing to the emerging complexities of health systems. Schools, workplaces, and community organizations can be vital in promoting and facilitating vaccination, especially for adolescents and adults. This approach enhances acceptability, ensures accessibility, reduces barriers, and improves coverage rates. School-based vaccination programs can be expanded to include vaccines for older children and adolescents, ensuring that this age group is protected against VPDs. LCI integration requires ongoing education and awareness campaigns to shift the public’s perception of vaccination from a childhood-only activity to a lifelong health behavior. Healthcare providers must be trained to deliver age-appropriate vaccination messages and to address vaccine hesitancy in all age groups. Public health campaigns should emphasize the benefits of a life course approach as new vaccines are introduced for the ageing population. To do so, countries need to allocate adequate resources to procure vaccines, regularly train healthcare workers, enhance infrastructure, and run public awareness campaigns. Incorporating expanded immunization services into health insurance schemes ensures equitable vaccine access, particularly for marginalized and vulnerable populations. Academic institutions and research bodies are indispensable for providing evidence-based guidance and evaluating the effectiveness of immunization programs. Strong partnerships with the private sector, particularly with pharmaceutical companies and technology firms, ensure the availability, affordability, and effective monitoring of vaccines through data-driven platforms. Public engagement is another critical component. Effective communication strategies must address vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, particularly among adults and the older adults. Involving community leaders and influencers can help build trust and acceptance, particularly when introducing vaccines for new age groups. Robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, tracking vaccine coverage and disease prevalence, are essential. These systems should track vaccine coverage, disease incidence, and health outcomes across age groups, providing data to identify gaps and refine strategies, and creating demand. Regular assessments ensure that immunization programs remain responsive to the population’s changing needs. Aligning national policies with global frameworks, such as IA 2030 and WHO’s strategies for healthy ageing, enables countries to benefit from shared resources and technical support while advancing global health goals.Systemic barriers and perceptions exist amongst adult and older adults cohorts. Immunization coverage among adults and the older adults faces unique challenges shaped by biological, social, and systemic factors. As age-associated vulnerability increases, vaccines are critical for these populations. Gaps in vaccination programs, limited awareness, and logistical barriers often hinder access and acceptance of vaccines in these cohorts. These challenges are compounded by the underrepresentation of adult and older adults immunization in national health strategies. Among the barriers to adult and older adults immunization, vaccine hesitancy and resistance remain significant obstacles. These issues are often rooted in longstanding beliefs, perceptions, and mistrust in the healthcare systems. Many adults and older individuals perceive vaccines as primary preventive tools for children, leading to a diminished sense of urgency about immunization in later life. This misconception is particularly evident with vaccines such as those for influenza, pneumococcal disease, and shingles, which are vital for protecting against severe illnesses but remain underutilized (67).Misconceptions about vaccine safety and efficacy can persist and intensify without clear, accessible information. Public health campaigns should highlight the role of vaccines in reducing hospitalizations, preventing complications, and supporting healthy ageing. Community leaders, faith-based influencers, and civil society groups must be mobilized to build trust, combat vaccine hesitancy, and address social and cultural barriers. NGOs and patient advocacy groups play a crucial role in outreach, advocacy, and education, helping to ensure that all segments of the population, especially the vulnerable, are reached (68). Fear of adverse events following immunization (AEFIs) also poses a significant barrier to vaccine acceptance among older populations. Even mild or moderate AEFIs can deter future vaccination, particularly for individuals with heightened health concerns. Addressing these fears requires transparent communication about the risks and benefits of vaccines. Developing robust monitoring systems for AEFIs and equipping healthcare providers with the tools to manage and reassure patients are critical to building trust and confidence in immunization (69).The development and delivery of vaccines for adults and the older adults must also account for age-related changes in immune function. Formulations that are both effective and well-tolerated are essential to ensure uptake. However, the success of these vaccines ultimately depends on demand generation through targeted education and outreach efforts. Healthcare providers play a pivotal role in this process, engaging in meaningful conversations with beneficiaries, addressing their concerns, and reinforcing the importance of immunization in preventing severe illness and maintaining quality of life. By addressing these interconnected challenges—systemic gaps, hesitancy, misinformation, and fear of AEFIs—immunization programs can better serve adult and older adults populations.The COVID-19 pandemic has provided critical insights into the importance of LCI. The rapid development and global rollout of COVID-19 vaccines highlighted the need for vaccination strategies that extend beyond childhood and target all age groups (70). The pandemic highlighted the vulnerabilities of older adults and those with underlying health conditions, who faced higher risks of severe illness and death from COVID-19. This situation demonstrated the need for integrated adult and older adults vaccination programs within routine healthcare services. The success of COVID-19 vaccination efforts in reducing hospitalizations and mortality among these populations emphasizes the value of an LCA in ensuring continuous protection against VPDs (71, 72).Significant challenges related to vaccine hesitancy, particularly among adults and the older adults, emerged strongly. The spread of misinformation, coupled with pre-existing mistrust in vaccines, led to varying levels of vaccine acceptance across different demographic groups. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that effective communication strategies and community engagement are essential for overcoming hesitancy and ensuring high vaccine uptake across the life course. Vaccine inequity and distribution emerged as another critical lesson. The disparities observed in vaccine access and uptake highlighted the need for policies that ensure equitable access for all age groups, particularly marginalized populations (73). Logistical challenges, such as the need for cold chain infrastructure and extensive coordination, emerged during the COVID-19 vaccination rollout. These challenges highlight the need for health systems to be resilient and adaptable and respond adequately to public health emergencies. Building such capacity is essential for successfully implementing LCI. The pandemic also reinforced the importance of global collaboration in vaccine development and distribution. International cooperation and shared resources enabled the unprecedented speed at which COVID-19 vaccines were developed, tested, and distributed. This collaborative approach is equally critical for the successful implementation of LCI, as it requires ongoing research, development, and the sharing of best practices to address the evolving landscape of VPDs.India’s immunization efforts have made significant progress in providing vaccines for twelve preventable diseases (74). However, this program has primarily focused on childhood vaccination and immunization for pregnant women, leaving considerable gaps in coverage across the life course. The comprehensive integration of LCI presents an opportunity to strengthen further efforts in addressing current and emerging public health challenges (12). Some state-level initiatives have expanded immunization to include adolescents and adults in recent years. Healthcare workers are prioritized for Hepatitis B vaccination due to their occupational risks. Japanese encephalitis vaccines are administered to adults in endemic states of the country, and tetanus and diphtheria (Td) vaccines are routinely given to pregnant women to safeguard maternal and neonatal health under UIP (75). Many vaccines for adults, such as Hepatitis B, typhoid, influenza, pneumococcal, and shingles, are available through the private healthcare sector, where their high cost limits uptake, leading to disparities. To accelerate the elimination of tuberculosis, the Government of India launched the “Adult BCG Vaccination Study” in 2024 under the National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP), aligning with tuberculosis eradication (76). The study aims to assess the effectiveness of the BCG vaccine in adults, expanding its use beyond childhood immunization, where it is already part of the UIP. While this represents significant progress, developing comprehensive national guidelines for adult vaccination is crucial. Establishing such frameworks would promote a more inclusive immunization strategy.The growing burden of VPDs among adolescents and adults in several LMICs, including India, underlines the need for a more comprehensive immunization strategy. There has been an increase in typhoid cases in recent years due to several factors, such as increased urbanization, AMR, and the impact of climate change (77). These highlight an opportunity to strengthen immunization efforts by adding new vaccines and booster doses, particularly among adolescents and adults. Vaccines like pneumococcal and shingles, recommended for older adults in many countries, are not yet systematically included in India’s public health programs despite their clear benefits in preventing hospitalizations and deaths.Adolescence is a critical life stage for immunization, as immunity against certain diseases wanes during this period, requiring booster doses to sustain protection. During adolescence, booster doses of tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccines can help maintain immunity and protect against these diseases. The HPV vaccine, which has demonstrated efficacy in preventing cervical cancer, is administered to adolescent girls through a nationwide campaign. Maternal immunization also plays a vital role in protecting both mothers and newborns. Yet, opportunities exist to expand coverage beyond tetanus to include other vaccines, such as influenza, which can provide additional protection against respiratory infections. The absence of a robust adult vaccination program results in inadequate protection against VPDs for adults and older populations, further compounded by high vaccine costs and limited awareness of their benefits. To address these gaps, the NTAGI has recommended incorporating the typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) into the routine immunization program, improving affordability and coverage, and reducing disease burden (78). Expanding the scope of LCI in India would also include critical vaccines like pneumococcal, shingles, and influenza, which could significantly reduce morbidity and healthcare costs (79). However, countries like India may not need to introduce all WHO-recommended vaccines. The country would rather benefit more from disease burden and surveillance-informed data across age cohorts and competing priorities. The economic benefits of vaccination extend beyond individual health to include reductions in healthcare expenditures and lower burdens on public health infrastructure, particularly during disease outbreaks. Implementing LCI in India requires comprehensive systemic reforms, including expanding the existing immunization framework to cover all age groups, introducing new vaccines, and establishing platform-based regulatory models to enable the swift introduction and scale-up of vaccines.India stands at a critical juncture in its public health landscape, where adopting LCI policies can be transformative in addressing the rising burden of VPDs. India has built a strong foundation that can now be expanded to encompass all age groups. The COVID-19 pandemic has reinforced the need for integrated life course vaccination policies to respond to emerging health threats (80). India’s preparedness is underpinned by its existing strengths. It is the largest vaccine manufacturer in the world, with extensive production capabilities and an expanding network of healthcare delivery points from primary to tertiary levels. India is known for its proficiency in manufacturing cost-effective vaccines and executing large-scale operations using the most advanced technology (81, 82). The country can achieve self-sufficiency in meeting its increasing demand for lifecourse vaccines. Additionally, the government’s commitment to immunization programs is e…

This can be achieved by integrating vaccines into the CPHC framework by aligning vaccination schedules with other routine health services such as maternal and child health visits, school health programs, and geriatric care for older adults. This integration promotes a seamless transition between different life stages, ensuring that vaccination remains a continuous priority throughout a person’s life. One way to achieve this integration is to leverage existing systems, such as electronic health records (EHRs) and immunization registries, to track vaccination status throughout a person’s lifetime. These systems can be linked with other health services, such as screenings and chronic disease management, to ensure that vaccination is part of a broader preventive health strategy. For instance, when an adult visits a clinic for a routine health check-up, their vaccination status can be reviewed, and any missing vaccines recommended for adults can be administered with consent, reinforcing the importance of immunization at every stage of life. Vaccination coverage in the second year of life is often lower than in the first year. Implementation challenges are observed in the second year of life owing to the sub-optimal orientation of the frontline workers to new targets and delivery modes–this also applies to adolescent vaccination (64). In 2024, India launched UWIN, a name-based digital registry system to enhance the immunization program through efficient tracking and real-time monitoring. The platform also offers a self-registration feature for all eligible citizens. UWIN is inspired by the success of COWIN, a platform that boosted vaccination rates among adults and the older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. This technological integration will pave the way for future lifecourse vaccines in the country (65, 66).Multi-sectoral stakeholder engagement requires attention owing to the emerging complexities of health systems. Schools, workplaces, and community organizations can be vital in promoting and facilitating vaccination, especially for adolescents and adults. This approach enhances acceptability, ensures accessibility, reduces barriers, and improves coverage rates. School-based vaccination programs can be expanded to include vaccines for older children and adolescents, ensuring that this age group is protected against VPDs. LCI integration requires ongoing education and awareness campaigns to shift the public’s perception of vaccination from a childhood-only activity to a lifelong health behavior. Healthcare providers must be trained to deliver age-appropriate vaccination messages and to address vaccine hesitancy in all age groups. Public health campaigns should emphasize the benefits of a life course approach as new vaccines are introduced for the ageing population. To do so, countries need to allocate adequate resources to procure vaccines, regularly train healthcare workers, enhance infrastructure, and run public awareness campaigns. Incorporating expanded immunization services into health insurance schemes ensures equitable vaccine access, particularly for marginalized and vulnerable populations. Academic institutions and research bodies are indispensable for providing evidence-based guidance and evaluating the effectiveness of immunization programs. Strong partnerships with the private sector, particularly with pharmaceutical companies and technology firms, ensure the availability, affordability, and effective monitoring of vaccines through data-driven platforms. Public engagement is another critical component. Effective communication strategies must address vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, particularly among adults and the older adults. Involving community leaders and influencers can help build trust and acceptance, particularly when introducing vaccines for new age groups. Robust monitoring and evaluation mechanisms, tracking vaccine coverage and disease prevalence, are essential. These systems should track vaccine coverage, disease incidence, and health outcomes across age groups, providing data to identify gaps and refine strategies, and creating demand. Regular assessments ensure that immunization programs remain responsive to the population’s changing needs. Aligning national policies with global frameworks, such as IA 2030 and WHO’s strategies for healthy ageing, enables countries to benefit from shared resources and technical support while advancing global health goals.Systemic barriers and perceptions exist amongst adult and older adults cohorts. Immunization coverage among adults and the older adults faces unique challenges shaped by biological, social, and systemic factors. As age-associated vulnerability increases, vaccines are critical for these populations. Gaps in vaccination programs, limited awareness, and logistical barriers often hinder access and acceptance of vaccines in these cohorts. These challenges are compounded by the underrepresentation of adult and older adults immunization in national health strategies. Among the barriers to adult and older adults immunization, vaccine hesitancy and resistance remain significant obstacles. These issues are often rooted in longstanding beliefs, perceptions, and mistrust in the healthcare systems. Many adults and older individuals perceive vaccines as primary preventive tools for children, leading to a diminished sense of urgency about immunization in later life. This misconception is particularly evident with vaccines such as those for influenza, pneumococcal disease, and shingles, which are vital for protecting against severe illnesses but remain underutilized (67).Misconceptions about vaccine safety and efficacy can persist and intensify without clear, accessible information. Public health campaigns should highlight the role of vaccines in reducing hospitalizations, preventing complications, and supporting healthy ageing. Community leaders, faith-based influencers, and civil society groups must be mobilized to build trust, combat vaccine hesitancy, and address social and cultural barriers. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionIndia’s changing demographic and disease profile provides a strong rationale for moving toward a life-course approach to immunization, while recognizing that childhood immunization must remain a core priority. India already has health-system platforms that can reach adolescents, adults, and older adults through routine health and community services. However, expansion should be gradual and guided by evidence on disease burden, vaccine effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, equity, affordability and implementation feasibility. India-specific economic evaluations and existing health programs can help identify which vaccines and population groups to prioritize. A well-planned approach can strengthen preventive health across the life course without creating parallel systems or placing avoidable pressure on frontline health workers. The next step is to generate stronger India-specific evidence and develop a clear, prioritized and sustainable framework for life-course immunization.5.1LimitationThis review has some limitations that should be considered when interpreting and correlating the findings. First, although the manuscript discusses the potential role of immunization across the life course, it does not undertake a formal economic evaluation or costing of an adult vaccination program in India. The financial implications would depend on the vaccines considered, target population, coverage, vaccine prices, delivery platforms, human-resource requirements, and supply-chain arrangements, and these parameters may vary considerably across different implementation models. Similarly, the review does not quantify the additional workload a life-course approach may place on frontline health workers, as this depends on how and at what level adult vaccination is integrated into the existing health system. Second, the strength of evidence is not uniform across all adult vaccines and population groups; therefore, the narrative should not be interpreted as implying that all adult vaccines have the same level of evidence, effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, or priority for inclusion in the national program. Future research should include India-specific costing, workforce and implementation assessments, and vaccine-specific evaluations to better understand the resource implications, feasibility, and potential opportunity costs of expanding immunization across the life course.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionThe global eradication of smallpox in 1980, following a landmark call to action by the World Health Assembly, remains a remarkable achievement. Building on this momentum, the 1974 launch of the “Expanded Program on Immunization” (EPI) galvanized nations to establish national immunization programs (1). This initiative adopted a “pediatric approach,” focusing primarily on immunizing children and pregnant women to reduce childhood morbidity and mortality. Gradually, the breadth of protection (BOP) against Vaccine Preventable Diseases (VPDs) was extended beyond childhood to adolescents and adults for certain diseases across the countries. Marking its 50th anniversary in 2024, the EPI represents a transformative milestone in global public health (2). There have been massive improvements in childhood health and vaccination coverage indicators; however, there is a need to expand efforts beyond childhood and ensure the benefits of immunization are provided across the life course—a life course approach (LCA). Vaccines were introduced to adolescents, adults, and older adults cohorts in different regions and countries at different times; however, the number and reach of such vaccines vary significantly across regions, and coverage remains sub-optimal, primarily in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) (3).1.1Global demographic shiftThe global population is ageing at an unprecedented rate. According to the United Nations (UN) Decade of Healthy Ageing Report 2021–30, by 2030, adults over 60 will outnumber adolescents and young adults, and one out of every six people is estimated to be 60 or older (4). The population of older adults is projected to grow by 34% by 2030 and double to 2.1 billion by 2050 (5). This demographic shift poses challenges for public health systems in promoting healthy ageing. Global life expectancy has increased from 66.0 in 2000 to 72.6 in 2019 and is expected to rise to 77.1 by 2050 (6). This shift is accompanied by a rising prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). While NCDs affect individuals across all age groups, their burden is disproportionately higher among older adults due to the accumulation of risk factors, and they become more susceptible to VPDs, disease severity, and complications (7). Ageing is associated with immunosenescence—a gradual functional decline of the immune system that makes older adults more susceptible to infectious diseases. The Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA 2030) also envisions universal access to vaccines across the life course to combat VPDs and strengthen health systems (8).The rising burden of VPDs highlights the need to expand vaccination programs across the life course to benefit vulnerable populations and alleviate strain on healthcare systems. Global data show that adult immunization significantly reduces the incidence of VPDs and associated healthcare costs (9). Older adults are particularly susceptible to diseases such as influenza, pneumococcal pneumonia, and shingles due to the natural decline of the immune system with age. Vaccination in this age group is vital to reduce morbidity and mortality. Coverage rates vary across WHO regions and are generally higher in high-income countries due to a more robust healthcare infrastructure (10).The life course approach is a multidisciplinary model that emphasizes dynamic interactions of biological, social, and environmental factors throughout one’s lifetime, influencing health outcomes (11). This approach holds importance given the demographic shift toward increased longevity and persistent social inequalities in health, emphasizing vaccination at every stage—from birth to old age to ensure individuals receive timely immunizations to protect against age-specific diseases. It recognizes that immune responses to vaccines vary by age and several other factors; hence, vaccinating individuals at appropriate ages provides optimal protection against VPDs. It is more important than ever to consider declining immunity in these populations to optimize vaccine effectiveness (12). However, adult vaccination uptake remains suboptimal among at-risk populations, and the life course approach to immunization is yet to be adopted in many countries, as most national immunization programs remain primarily focused on the pediatric population (3).1.2Disease profile and epidemiological aspects across the life courseThe evolving health risks and disease burden across different life stages—children, adolescents, adults, and the older adults present unique challenges and opportunities for vaccination. In 2022, approximately 18 million children worldwide missed the first dose of the DPT (diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus) vaccine, leaving them vulnerable to outbreaks and jeopardizing herd immunity. These gaps risk individual health and threaten population-level disease control in regions where VPDs have been contained to a large extent (13). Childhood vaccines such as DPT, with >90% efficacy, have significantly reduced global childhood mortality. Similarly, the measles vaccine, with two recommended doses, provides 97% protection, which is critical in outbreak prevention (14). However, diseases like meningococcal meningitis remain a significant threat to adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa, with “high-risk” in the “meningitis belt,” with large-scale frequent outbreaks every 5–12 years. Despite the evident need, immunization coverage among adolescents lags behind that of children, largely due to inadequate structured programs and insufficient awareness (15).While childhood immunization programs have achieved considerable progress, the prevalence of communicable and non-communicable diseases remains a concern among adults and the older adults. The older adults population is disproportionately affected by VPDs such as influenza, pneumococcal disease, and herpes zoster. Influenza alone accounts for up to 72,000 deaths annually among older adults in Europe (16). Pneumococcal disease remains a leading cause of severe pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis among older populations, particularly in regions with high rates of chronic respiratory illnesses. Although introducing pneumococcal vaccines into adult vaccination schedules has significantly reduced disease incidence, global coverage remains inadequate (17). Herpes zoster (Shingles) affects approximately one in three individuals during their lifetime and presents a significant health risk, particularly for older adults. Vaccination has been shown to effectively lower both the occurrence and the severity of this condition, offering critical protection to this vulnerable population (18). Globally, the integration of life course immunization (LCI) strategies varies widely. In high-income countries (HICs) like the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends vaccinations from infancy through older adulthood, including HPV for adolescents and pneumococcal vaccines for the older adults (19). Similarly, the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) emphasizes flu vaccines for children and older adults, while Japan has included pneumococcal vaccines for the older adults in its national immunization program. Australia’s comprehensive schedule incorporates vaccines like herpes zoster for older adults and HPV for adolescents (20). Hepatitis B affects over 296 million people globally, causing 820,000 deaths annually, primarily from liver disease and cancer. Hepatitis B vaccination is especially critical for high-risk groups, such as healthcare workers and individuals with chronic liver conditions (21, 22).In contrast, many developing countries remain focused on childhood immunization, with limited vaccine coverage for adolescents and adults. However, countries like Brazil and Mexico are bridging this gap by expanding their immunization programs to include these populations, signaling a growing recognition of LCI’s importance (23, 24). full_text: AbstractA 56-year-old man presented with a nine-month history of progressive left-sided nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial and palatal pain, and proptosis. Imaging demonstrated a large destructive left sinonasal mass extending into the left maxillary sinus and orbit. An endoscopic biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated epithelial malignancy, initially classified as a sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma (SNUC). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong cytokeratin expression and complete loss of integrase interactor 1 (INI1) nuclear expression in tumor cells, with retained staining in non-neoplastic elements.The patient underwent a left subtotal maxillectomy with hard palate resection. The tumor measured at least 8 cm, involved the pterygoid muscle, and extended to the medial and superior resection margins. Following surgery, he received platinum-based chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Approximately two years later, he presented with progressive exertional dyspnea. Imaging revealed a large left pleural effusion and bilateral soft-tissue-attenuation pulmonary nodules. Pleural fluid evaluation was nondiagnostic for malignancy because of limited cellularity; however, a computed tomography-guided core biopsy of a right pulmonary nodule revealed metastatic carcinoma morphologically concordant with the sinonasal primary, with strong cytokeratin expression and persistent loss of INI1.The patient subsequently received six cycles of pembrolizumab combined with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and vincristine. Comprehensive molecular profiling of archived primary tumor tissue later identified a pathogenic SMARCB1 copy-number deletion, establishing the diagnosis of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. At the last documented follow-up, fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) demonstrated persistent metabolically active thoracic metastatic disease without interval progression or new sites of disease. This case illustrates how integration of morphology, immunohistochemistry, metastatic-site comparison, and molecular testing can refine the classification of a poorly differentiated sinonasal carcinoma initially diagnosed as SNUC.Keywords: immunohistochemistry, ini1 loss, metastatic sinonasal carcinoma, molecular profiling, molecular reclassification, pulmonary metastasis, sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma, smarcb1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, smarcb1 deletion, swi/snf complex DiscussionSMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma is a rare, highly aggressive, molecularly defined subtype of SWI/SNF complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma that illustrates the increasing importance of molecular classification among poorly differentiated sinonasal tumors. Before recognition of SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma as a distinct entity, these neoplasms were frequently classified as SNUC, nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, or other poorly differentiated malignancies [1-5]. In the present case, the tumor was initially classified as SNUC based on its high-grade morphology and epithelial immunophenotype; however, the concurrent complete loss of INI1 represented an important diagnostic clue to SWI/SNF complex deficiency. Subsequent identification of a pathogenic SMARCB1 copy-number deletion enabled definitive molecular classification as SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma.Histologically, SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinomas commonly demonstrate basaloid or poorly differentiated morphology, with tumor cells arranged in solid nests, sheets, or trabeculae and variably exhibiting rhabdoid cytologic features [3-7]. Necrosis and brisk mitotic activity may be prominent. This morphologic spectrum creates substantial overlap with other small round blue cell and undifferentiated tumors of the sinonasal tract. The differential diagnosis includes conventional SNUC, neuroendocrine carcinoma, NUT carcinoma, SMARCA4-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, olfactory neuroblastoma, lymphoma, melanoma, and sarcomas. In this case, diffuse cytokeratin expression established epithelial differentiation, whereas negative neuroendocrine, hematolymphoid, and myogenic markers, together with the absence of S100 expression, argued against several major mimics. Strong, diffuse p16 expression should not independently be interpreted as evidence of human papillomavirus-associated disease, as p16 overexpression is not specific in this setting. Similarly, the negative Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA (EBER) result did not support an Epstein-Barr virus-associated carcinoma.SMARCB1 encodes INI1, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. Loss of SMARCB1 function disrupts chromatin regulation and promotes oncogenesis through broad alterations in transcriptional control [3-5]. Genetic studies have demonstrated that homozygous SMARCB1 deletion is the most frequent mechanism underlying INI1 protein loss in these carcinomas, although hemizygous deletions and truncating alterations have also been identified [8]. Immunohistochemical loss of INI1, with retained staining in non-neoplastic internal controls, therefore provides a rapid and highly informative diagnostic finding. The complete absence of tumor-cell nuclear expression in both the sinonasal primary and pulmonary metastasis was particularly important in this case. Detection of a pathogenic SMARCB1 deletion in the archived primary tumor molecularly corroborated the immunophenotype and established a unifying diagnosis across specimens obtained approximately two years apart.The clinical course also reflects the aggressive behavior reported for this entity. SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinomas frequently present at an advanced local stage because of their anatomically confined site and nonspecific early symptoms [3-7,9,10]. The primary tumor in this patient measured at least 8 cm, involved the pterygoid muscle, and had positive medial and superior resection margins. Although neither lymphovascular nor perineural invasion was identified, the patient subsequently developed bilateral pulmonary nodules and a large pleural effusion. The initially sampled pleural fluid contained only rare, atypical epithelial cells and was insufficient for a definitive malignant diagnosis. In contrast, adequate core sampling of a right pulmonary nodule demonstrated a carcinoma morphologically and immunophenotypically concordant with the sinonasal primary. This distinction is clinically important because cytologically paucicellular effusions may be nondiagnostic, whereas tissue sampling can permit comparison of morphology and lineage-defining biomarkers.Because of its rarity, no universally accepted treatment algorithm has been established for SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. Management is generally multimodal and may include surgical resection followed by radiation, with concurrent or sequential platinum-based chemotherapy depending on disease extent and resectability [5,9,10]. The patient underwent an extensive surgical resection followed by 7,200 cGy of radiotherapy and nine cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy. Retrospective series suggest that aggressive multimodal therapy may provide locoregional control, but recurrence and distant metastasis remain common, and conclusions are limited by small sample sizes, treatment heterogeneity, and selection bias [9,10].Evidence supporting systemic therapy for recurrent or metastatic disease remains particularly limited. Published reports have described immune checkpoint inhibitors in selected patients with SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, but the small number of cases precludes reliable estimates of response or identification of predictive biomarkers [11]. In the present case, the patient began pembrolizumab in combination with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and vincristine before the molecular profiling results became available. Subsequent testing demonstrated that the tumor was microsatellite stable, had a low tumor mutational burden, and showed a PD-L1 combined positive score of 0. Follow-up FDG PET/CT demonstrated persistent metabolically active pleural metastatic disease without interval progression or new sites of disease. Because pembrolizumab was administered as part of a multidrug regimen, the contribution of any individual agent cannot be determined. Moreover, disease stability in a single patient should not be interpreted as evidence that conventional immune-response biomarkers are irrelevant in this tumor type.SMARCB1 loss also provides a potential therapeutic rationale for targeting enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a catalytic component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 that functionally opposes SWI/SNF activity. Tazemetostat, an EZH2 inhibitor, has demonstrated clinical activity in advanced epithelioid sarcoma with INI1 loss [12]. However, those data cannot be directly extrapolated to SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, and the role of EZH2 inhibition in this disease remains investigational. Collaborative molecularly informed trials will be necessary to evaluate such targeted approaches in this exceptionally uncommon malignancy. Pulmonary metastasis of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma has previously been described as a diagnostic pitfall, emphasizing the importance of clinical history, morphologic comparison with the primary tumor, and INI1 immunohistochemistry when evaluating a poorly differentiated carcinoma in the lung [13].This case highlights three practical lessons. First, complete INI1 loss should prompt consideration of SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma whenever a poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancy is encountered. Second, re-evaluation of an earlier nonspecific diagnosis may be warranted when new immunohistochemical or molecular information becomes available. Finally, comparison of the primary and metastatic tumors, including morphology, epithelial markers, and INI1 expression, can establish the origin of distant disease and directly affect classification, prognostication, and treatment planning. ConclusionsSMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancy, particularly when the initial findings suggest SNUC. Complete loss of INI1 expression, supported when available by molecular confirmation of SMARCB1 alteration, enables accurate classification and distinction from morphologically overlapping entities. In this patient, concordant morphology and INI1 loss in the primary tumor and pulmonary metastasis established the origin of the distant disease approximately two years after the original diagnosis. This case underscores the aggressive behavior of this rare carcinoma, the value of adequate tissue sampling at recurrence, and the importance of reassessing earlier diagnoses as molecular classifications evolve. Although the patient had persistent metabolically active metastatic disease without interval progression at the last documented follow-up following combination systemic therapy, the optimal management of metastatic SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma remains undefined and requires further collaborative investigation. IntroductionHigh-grade sinonasal carcinomas comprise a heterogeneous group of malignant epithelial neoplasms with overlapping morphologic and immunophenotypic features. Historically, tumors lacking definitive squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation were often classified as sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma (SNUC), a diagnosis of exclusion. Advances in immunohistochemistry and molecular profiling have distinguished several biologically discrete entities or molecular subsets within this group, including nuclear protein in testis (NUT) carcinoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2)-mutant SNUC, and switch/sucrose nonfermentable (SWI/SNF) complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma [1,2]. The latter category encompasses tumors characterized by deficiency of either SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 [2].SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, a molecularly defined subtype of SWI/SNF complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, was first characterized as a distinct entity in 2014 [3,4]. It is characterized by complete loss of nuclear integrase interactor 1 (INI1) expression, the protein encoded by the tumor-suppressor gene SMARCB1, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. Histologically, these tumors frequently demonstrate basaloid or rhabdoid cytomorphology arranged in nests, sheets, or cords, often without specific squamous or glandular differentiation. Their morphologic heterogeneity and variable immunophenotype may lead to classification as SNUC or other poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancies, particularly with limited biopsy material [3-5]. Recognition of INI1 loss is therefore an important diagnostic clue that should prompt molecular correlation when available.We present a SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma initially classified as SNUC in a 56-year-old man who subsequently developed pulmonary metastatic disease. Complete loss of INI1 expression was present in the initial biopsy, resection specimen, and pulmonary metastasis, while comprehensive molecular profiling of the primary tumor identified a pathogenic SMARCB1 copy-number deletion. Although this reclassification did not alter the treatment already administered in this case, accurate identification has diagnostic and prognostic significance and may inform consideration of molecularly guided therapeutic strategies or clinical trials [6]. This case illustrates the value of integrating morphology, immunohistochemistry, comparison of primary and metastatic specimens, and molecular profiling to refine the classification and clinical assessment of poorly differentiated sinonasal carcinomas. Case presentationA 56-year-old man with a medical history of essential hypertension treated with oral antihypertensives was evaluated for a nine-month history of progressive left-sided nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, facial and palatal pain with paresthesia, headaches, rhinorrhea, and left-sided epiphora. Physical examination demonstrated mild left proptosis with preserved extraocular movements, bulging of the left hard palate, and a left nasal cavity mass draining serosanguineous fluid. No cervical lymphadenopathy was identified. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a large, locally invasive mass centered in the left nasal cavity, with significant osseous destruction and extension into the extraconal left orbit, maxillary sinus, ethmoidal air cells, and sphenoid sinus (Figure 1).Figure 1Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses.Axial (A) and coronal (B) images demonstrate a large, locally destructive left sinonasal mass (red asterisk) centered in the nasal cavity, with destructive extension into the adjacent ipsilateral paranasal sinuses and left extraconal orbit (solid blue arrow).Endoscopic examination revealed a highly vascular, rubbery left nasal cavity mass with focal cavitary areas. Multiple biopsies were obtained. Intraoperative consultation confirmed malignancy but deferred definitive classification pending immunohistochemical evaluation. Histologic examination demonstrated a poorly differentiated epithelial malignancy composed predominantly of basaloid cells arranged in solid sheets, with associated necrosis and stromal reaction (Figure 2).Figure 2Histopathologic features of the primary sinonasal tumor.Hematoxylin and eosin staining demonstrates a poorly differentiated carcinoma arranged in solid nests and sheets, with associated tumor necrosis (straight blue arrow) and fibrous stromal septa (curved blue arrow) (20×).The tumor showed strong, diffuse expression of cytokeratin 8/18, patchy pancytokeratin and cytokeratin 7 expression, strong, diffuse p16 staining, and focal expression of neuron-specific enolase. It was negative for cluster of differentiation (CD)45, CD99, chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100, cytokeratin 5/6, p40, p63, cellular-KIT (c-KIT), and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA. INI1 immunohistochemistry demonstrated complete loss of nuclear expression in tumor cells, with retained staining in non-neoplastic stromal elements serving as an internal positive control (Figure 3).Figure 3Immunohistochemical findings of the primary sinonasal tumor.(A) The tumor cells demonstrate strong, patchy pancytokeratin expression, confirming epithelial differentiation (20×). (B) INI1 immunohistochemistry shows complete loss of nuclear expression in the tumor cells, with retained nuclear staining in non-neoplastic stromal elements serving as an internal positive control (10×). INI1: integrase interactor 1.Based on the morphologic and immunophenotypic findings available at the time, the lesion was initially classified as SNUC.Approximately seven weeks after the biopsy, the patient underwent a left lateral rhinotomy with subtotal maxillectomy, hard palate resection, extranasal ethmoidectomy, sphenoidotomy, and resection of the tumor and pterygoid plates. The fragmented tumor measured at least 8 cm and extensively involved the left maxillary sinus. Histologic examination demonstrated an extensively invasive, poorly differentiated carcinoma with solid growth, geographic necrosis, and fibrotic stroma (Figure 4).Figure 4Histopathologic features of the primary tumor resection.(A) Low-power hematoxylin and eosin view showing carcinoma arranged in solid nests and sheets with confluent geographic necrosis (straight blue arrows) and intervening stromal fibrosis (curved blue arrows). Occasional cells exhibit eccentrically located nuclei and more abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, imparting focal rhabdoid features (40x).Tumor involvement of the left pterygoid muscle was identified. In this case, diffuse cytokeratin expression established epithelial differentiation, whereas negative neuroendocrine, hematolymphoid, and myogenic markers, together with the absence of S100 expression, argued against several major mimics. Strong, diffuse p16 expression should not independently be interpreted as evidence of human papillomavirus-associated disease, as p16 overexpression is not specific in this setting. Similarly, the negative Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA (EBER) result did not support an Epstein-Barr virus-associated carcinoma.SMARCB1 encodes INI1, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. Loss of SMARCB1 function disrupts chromatin regulation and promotes oncogenesis through broad alterations in transcriptional control [3-5]. Genetic studies have demonstrated that homozygous SMARCB1 deletion is the most frequent mechanism underlying INI1 protein loss in these carcinomas, although hemizygous deletions and truncating alterations have also been identified [8]. Immunohistochemical loss of INI1, with retained staining in non-neoplastic internal controls, therefore provides a rapid and highly informative diagnostic finding. The complete absence of tumor-cell nuclear expression in both the sinonasal primary and pulmonary metastasis was particularly important in this case. Detection of a pathogenic SMARCB1 deletion in the archived primary tumor molecularly corroborated the immunophenotype and established a unifying diagnosis across specimens obtained approximately two years apart.The clinical course also reflects the aggressive behavior reported for this entity. SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinomas frequently present at an advanced local stage because of their anatomically confined site and nonspecific early symptoms [3-7,9,10]. The primary tumor in this patient measured at least 8 cm, involved the pterygoid muscle, and had positive medial and superior resection margins. Although neither lymphovascular nor perineural invasion was identified, the patient subsequently developed bilateral pulmonary nodules and a large pleural effusion. The initially sampled pleural fluid contained only rare, atypical epithelial cells and was insufficient for a definitive malignant diagnosis. In contrast, adequate core sampling of a right pulmonary nodule demonstrated a carcinoma morphologically and immunophenotypically concordant with the sinonasal primary. This distinction is clinically important because cytologically paucicellular effusions may be nondiagnostic, whereas tissue sampling can permit comparison of morphology and lineage-defining biomarkers.Because of its rarity, no universally accepted treatment algorithm has been established for SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. Management is generally multimodal and may include surgical resection followed by radiation, with concurrent or sequential platinum-based chemotherapy depending on disease extent and resectability [5,9,10]. The patient underwent an extensive surgical resection followed by 7,200 cGy of radiotherapy and nine cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy. Retrospective series suggest that aggressive multimodal therapy may provide locoregional control, but recurrence and distant metastasis remain common, and conclusions are limited by small sample sizes, treatment heterogeneity, and selection bias [9,10].Evidence supporting systemic therapy for recurrent or metastatic disease remains particularly limited. Published reports have described immune checkpoint inhibitors in selected patients with SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, but the small number of cases precludes reliable estimates of response or identification of predictive biomarkers [11]. In the present case, the patient began pembrolizumab in combination with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and vincristine before the molecular profiling results became available. Subsequent testing demonstrated that the tumor was microsatellite stable, had a low tumor mutational burden, and showed a PD-L1 combined positive score of 0. Follow-up FDG PET/CT demonstrated persistent metabolically active pleural metastatic disease without interval progression or new sites of disease. Because pembrolizumab was administered as part of a multidrug regimen, the contribution of any individual agent cannot be determined. Moreover, disease stability in a single patient should not be interpreted as evidence that conventional immune-response biomarkers are irrelevant in this tumor type.SMARCB1 loss also provides a potential therapeutic rationale for targeting enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a catalytic component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 that functionally opposes SWI/SNF activity. Tazemetostat, an EZH2 inhibitor, has demonstrated clinical activity in advanced epithelioid sarcoma with INI1 loss [12]. However, those data cannot be directly extrapolated to SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, and the role of EZH2 inhibition in this disease remains investigational. Collaborative molecularly informed trials will be necessary to evaluate such targeted approaches in this exceptionally uncommon malignancy. Pulmonary metastasis of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma has previously been described as a diagnostic pitfall, emphasizing the importance of clinical history, morphologic comparison with the primary tumor, and INI1 immunohistochemistry when evaluating a poorly differentiated carcinoma in the lung [13].This case highlights three practical lessons. First, complete INI1 loss should prompt consideration of SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma whenever a poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancy is encountered. Second, re-evaluation of an earlier nonspecific diagnosis may be warranted when new immunohistochemical or molecular information becomes available. Finally, comparison of the primary and metastatic tumors, including morphology, epithelial markers, and INI1 expression, can establish the origin of distant disease and directly affect classification, prognostication, and treatment planning.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsSMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancy, particularly when the initial findings suggest SNUC. Complete loss of INI1 expression, supported when available by molecular confirmation of SMARCB1 alteration, enables accurate classification and distinction from morphologically overlapping entities. In this patient, concordant morphology and INI1 loss in the primary tumor and pulmonary metastasis established the origin of the distant disease approximately two years after the original diagnosis. This case underscores the aggressive behavior of this rare carcinoma, the value of adequate tissue sampling at recurrence, and the importance of reassessing earlier diagnoses as molecular classifications evolve. Although the patient had persistent metabolically active metastatic disease without interval progression at the last documented follow-up following combination systemic therapy, the optimal management of metastatic SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma remains undefined and requires further collaborative investigation.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHigh-grade sinonasal carcinomas comprise a heterogeneous group of malignant epithelial neoplasms with overlapping morphologic and immunophenotypic features. Historically, tumors lacking definitive squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation were often classified as sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma (SNUC), a diagnosis of exclusion. Advances in immunohistochemistry and molecular profiling have distinguished several biologically discrete entities or molecular subsets within this group, including nuclear protein in testis (NUT) carcinoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2)-mutant SNUC, and switch/sucrose nonfermentable (SWI/SNF) complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma [1,2]. The latter category encompasses tumors characterized by deficiency of either SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 [2].SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, a molecularly defined subtype of SWI/SNF complex-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, was first characterized as a distinct entity in 2014 [3,4]. It is characterized by complete loss of nuclear integrase interactor 1 (INI1) expression, the protein encoded by the tumor-suppressor gene SMARCB1, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. Histologically, these tumors frequently demonstrate basaloid or rhabdoid cytomorphology arranged in nests, sheets, or cords, often without specific squamous or glandular differentiation. Their morphologic heterogeneity and variable immunophenotype may lead to classification as SNUC or other poorly differentiated sinonasal malignancies, particularly with limited biopsy material [3-5]. Recognition of INI1 loss is therefore an important diagnostic clue that should prompt molecular correlation when available.We present a SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma initially classified as SNUC in a 56-year-old man who subsequently developed pulmonary metastatic disease. Complete loss of INI1 expression was present in the initial biopsy, resection specimen, and pulmonary metastasis, while comprehensive molecular profiling of the primary tumor identified a pathogenic SMARCB1 copy-number deletion. Although this reclassification did not alter the treatment already administered in this case, accurate identification has diagnostic and prognostic significance and may inform consideration of molecularly guided therapeutic strategies or clinical trials [6]. This case illustrates the value of integrating morphology, immunohistochemistry, comparison of primary and metastatic specimens, and molecular profiling to refine the classification and clinical assessment of poorly differentiated sinonasal carcinomas. full_text: Cervical cancer remains a predominant malignancy of the female reproductive system and a critical global health challenge. Traditional platinum-based agents such as cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin, are cornerstones in postoperative adjuvant therapy, management of locally advanced cases, and systemic treatment of recurrent/metastatic disease. However, their clinical efficacy is frequently hampered by severe systemic toxicities and the emergence of chemoresistance. To address these bottlenecks, diverse nano-delivery platforms have been engineered to enhance bioavailability and mitigate adverse effects. This review systematically delineates the evolution of first-to third-generation platinum drugs, elucidating their molecular mechanisms of action specifically within the landscape of cervical cancer. Furthermore, we critically evaluate the clinical application of these agents and provide a comprehensive synthesis of recent advances in nano-delivery systems, including targeted and stimuli-responsive carriers. By bridging traditional pharmacology with cutting-edge nanotechnology, this review offers strategic insights into achieving precise delivery and controlled release, potentially defining new paradigms for the next-generation of cervical cancer therapeutics. 6ConclusionAs a fundamental drug for anti-tumor treatment, platinum-based drugs hold an irreplaceable core position in the cervical cancer treatment system, and play a crucial role in postoperative adjuvant therapy, intervention for locally advanced lesions, and systematic management of recurrent or metastatic lesions. The traditional platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin and oxaliplatin) have established a solid foundation of clinical efficacy. However, their inherent systemic toxicity and acquired drug resistance remain issues limit the maximization of their efficacy and their long-term application. Based on the cross-innovation of molecular pharmacology and nanotechnology, the application research of platinum-based drugs in the cervical cancer treatment has achieved multi-dimensional breakthroughs, bringing exciting opportunities for the better clinical application of platinum drugs: (i) The use of tree-like macromolecules, liposomes and metal-organic frameworks as carriers enables the precise targeted delivery and controlled release of platinum drugs, reducing systemic toxicity. (ii) The tumor-targeted delivery systems are constructed to introduce cervical cancer-specific targeting moieties (e.g., integrin-recognition peptides and folate receptor ligands), significantly enhancing the enrichment efficiency of drugs in cervical tumor tissues. At the same time, tumor microenvironment-responsive elements are integrated to enable the precise activation and release of drugs locally in tumors, thereby effectively reducing damage to normal tissues. (iii) Develop platinum-DNA cross-linking repair inhibitors, polynuclear platinum complexes, and combine them with PARP inhibitors or epigenetic drugs to break through the resistance barrier. (IV) The construction of platinum-containing radioactive probes or fluorescent markers enables precise identification of cervical tumor lesions, providing precise imaging evidence for the early diagnosis and staging assessment of cervical cancer. At the same time, it enables real-time monitoring of the dynamic changes of tumor tissues during the treatment process, achieving true integration of diagnosis and treatment. Through sustained pharmacological exploration and interdisciplinary technological integration, the future development of platinum-based drugs in the treatment of cervical cancer will continue to advance towards the directions of high efficiency, low toxicity, precision and intelligence, thereby providing better solutions to improve patient prognosis. 1IntroductionCervical cancer is one of the common malignancies that pose a significant threat to women’s life and health, with a particularly high incidence among women aged 35-40 (Francoeur et al., 2025). In recent years, cervical cancer screening and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination have alleviated the incidence of cervical cancer to a certain extent, but its incidence rate still ranks first among malignancies of the female reproductive system, and exhibits a trend toward youthfulness. According to the latest GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates released in 2024, there were approximately 661044 new cases and 348186 deaths globally (Bray et al., 2024). Although it ranks fourth among the most common cancers in women worldwide, cervical cancer remains the most prevalent malignant tumor of the female reproductive system in many developing countries, and nearly 90% of deaths worldwide occur in low- and middle-income countries. Currently, clinical interventions for cervical cancer include surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, often supplemented by targeted therapy and immunotherapy (Ye et al., 2023). Among them, platinum-based chemotherapy regimens have always played an irreplaceable role in preventing postoperative recurrence, controlling locally advanced tumors, and providing systemic treatment for recurrent or metastatic lesions.Currently, the standard of systemic treatment for cervical cancer is highly dependent on tumor stage and pathological characteristics. For locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC), cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) remains the “gold standard” in clinical treatment. However, in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic disease, clinical practice has shifted towards more complex combination regimens, including the introduction of anti-angiogenic drugs (such as bevacizumab) or immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as pembrolizumab) (Liang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025).Based on their chemical structure and clinical applications, these drugs can be divided into three generations. Cisplatin remains the gold standard, while subsequent drugs such as carboplatin and oxaliplatin were developed to overcome their systemic toxicity and drug resistance issues (Dasari et al., 2022; de Vries et al., 2020; Song et al., 2022; Rades et al., 2023; Negi et al., 2020; Shahsavani et al., 2025; Dehghani et al., 2025). In addition to cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin, which are widely used globally, derivatives such as nedaplatin and lobaplatin are also being integrated into clinical practice in specific regions, such as East Asia, due to their unique toxicity characteristics. For example, carboplatin and oxaliplatin are often used in combination chemotherapy for relapsed or metastatic diseases to reduce systemic side effects in patients.Advances in nanotechnology and molecular pharmacology, nano-delivery systems can enhance the tumor specificity of drugs via both passive and active targeting approaches, while simultaneously improving the bioavailability, stability and targeting ability of therapeutics (Pan et al., 2022). The main strategies for conjugating platinum drug with delivery carriers include physical encapsulation, chemical covalent bonding, and electrostatic interaction. At present, platinum-based drugs can be conjugated with inorganic materials (e.g., carbon materials, mesoporous silica nanoparticles and gold nanomaterials) and organic materials (e.g., polymers, dendrimers, and liposomal micelles) via physical encapsulation, chemical covalent bonding, or electrostatic interaction to achieve drug delivery (Kapadne et al., 2024; Kalayil et al., 2024; Stępień et al., 2025; Santos et al., 2024) Despite the promise of nanotechnology, designing ideal delivery platforms for cervical cancer requires overcoming hurdles such as optimizing drug loading capacity, minimizing premature leakage in systemic circulation, and ensuring spatiotemporally controlled release at the tumor site. Nevertheless, the design of platinum-based drug delivery systems still faces the following challenges: high-efficiency drug loading capacity, reliable premature leakage prevention performance, precise lesion-targeting capability, and controllable drug release efficiency.This review provides a comprehensive overview on the development process, the anti-tumor mechanisms, and the mechanisms of drug resistance of platinum-based drugs. It also elaborates on the current clinical application status and optimization strategies of platinum-based metal drugs in the treatment of cervical cancer, aiming to provide references and insights for future translational medicine research on platinum-based drugs. 2Development process and antitumor mechanismGiven the significant role of platinum-based drugs in the treatment of cervical cancer, we summarize the evolutionary process of these drugs from accidental discovery to systematic development and present their anti-tumor mechanisms (Figure 1).FIGURE 1The structural evolution and clinical categorization of major platinum-based agents.Infographic showing three generations of platinum-based chemotherapy drugs: cisplatin as the first generation with global standard use, carboplatin and nedaplatin as second generation drugs for toxicity reduction, and oxaliplatin as the third generation for overcoming drug resistance. Blue and pink arrows below highlight systemic toxicity reduction and overcoming drug resistance through nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity reduction, DNA damage repair pathway blocking, and drug efflux reduction.2.1Cisplatin: discovery and the gold standard for CCRTCisplatin (cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2]) stands as the pioneering heavy metal coordination compound with broad-spectrum antitumor activity. Since its FDA approval in 1978, it has remained the global gold standard for concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) in cervical cancer (Peyrone, 1844; Rosenberg et al., 1969; Mitsunaga et al., 2011).The cytotoxic mechanism of cisplatin involves the formation of DNA cross-links that inhibit transcription and replication. Upon cellular entry via copper transporters (CTR1), the low intracellular chloride environment triggers the substitution of chloride ligands with water molecules, forming electrophilic aqua-complexes (Holzer et al., 2006) (Figure 2). These positively charged species are subsequently attracted to the negatively charged nuclear DNA and interact with the nucleophilic centers of DNA purine bases (specifically the N7 sites of guanine or adenine). The resulting platinum-DNA adducts bend and distort the DNA structure, inhibit transcription, trigger cell apoptosis, and ultimately lead to cell death (Rocha et al., 2018).FIGURE 2The structure and mechanisms of action of cisplatin (Browning et al., 2017).Illustration of the cellular uptake and action of cisplatin, a chemotherapy drug, showing its entry by passive diffusion or via CTR1 transporter, hydrolysis in reduced chloride environment, and binding to DNA leading to apoptosis if not repaired or resistance if repaired.Despite its clinical efficacy, cisplatin is limited by significant systemic toxicities, most notably nephrotoxicity, which affects approximately 30% of patients at standard therapeutic doses (50–75 mg/m2). Additional complications include neurotoxicity, ototoxicity, and myelosuppression, alongside the persistent challenge of intrinsic and acquired resistance (Chen and Chang, 2019).2.2Structural evolution for toxicity reduction: carboplatin and nedaplatinTo mitigate these adverse effects, second-generation analogues with modified leaving groups were developed to enhance patient tolerability. Carboplatin, characterized by the replacement of chloride ligands with a cyclobutene-1,1-dicarboxylate moiety, represents a significant advancement in structural optimization. This modification increases water solubility 16-fold and slows the drug’s activation kinetics, resulting in a substantially reduced incidence of nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and emesis compared to cisplatin (Calvert et al., 1982). While carboplatin is recognized as a global standard for patients with renal impairment or cisplatin intolerance, its clinical utility is often constrained by dose-limiting myelosuppression and cross-resistance with cisplatin, as both agents share the same diammine carrier group. Similarly, Nedaplatin features a glycolate leaving group that enhances solubility and reduces renal toxicity. Although integrated into clinical practice primarily in East Asia as a regional alternative for advanced or recurrent cases, nedaplatin exhibits a similar mechanism of DNA adduct formation and remains effective in some cisplatin-resistant phenotypes, though it has not reached universal standard status.2.3Structural evolution to overcome resistance: oxaliplatin and lobaplatinThe third evolutionary phase focused on bypassing the DNA repair mechanisms responsible for cisplatin resistance. Oxaliplatin incorporates a 1,2-diaminocyclohexane (DACH) ligand, which forms bulkier, more rigid DNA adducts compared to earlier generations. These unique adducts are less easily recognized and repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) system or mismatch repair (MMR) proteins, allowing oxaliplatin to maintain activity in cisplatin-resistant cell lines (Wheate et al., 2010; Quintão et al., 2019). Since its FDA approval in 2002, oxaliplatin has become a cornerstone in combination regimens for recurrent cervical cancer. Parallel to this, Lobaplatin-another DACH-containing derivative approved in China-offers an alternative for patients with established resistance or severe gastrointestinal intolerance to standard therapies.
