For locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC), cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) remains the “gold standard” in clinical treatment. However, in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic disease, clinical practice has shifted towards more complex combination regimens, including the introduction of anti-angiogenic drugs (such as bevacizumab) or immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as pembrolizumab) (Liang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025).Based on their chemical structure and clinical applications, these drugs can be divided into three generations. Cisplatin remains the gold standard, while subsequent drugs such as carboplatin and oxaliplatin were developed to overcome their systemic toxicity and drug resistance issues (Dasari et al., 2022; de Vries et al., 2020; Song et al., 2022; Rades et al., 2023; Negi et al., 2020; Shahsavani et al., 2025; Dehghani et al., 2025). In addition to cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin, which are widely used globally, derivatives such as nedaplatin and lobaplatin are also being integrated into clinical practice in specific regions, such as East Asia, due to their unique toxicity characteristics. For example, carboplatin and oxaliplatin are often used in combination chemotherapy for relapsed or metastatic diseases to reduce systemic side effects in patients.Advances in nanotechnology and molecular pharmacology, nano-delivery systems can enhance the tumor specificity of drugs via both passive and active targeting approaches, while simultaneously improving the bioavailability, stability and targeting ability of therapeutics (Pan et al., 2022). The main strategies for conjugating platinum drug with delivery carriers include physical encapsulation, chemical covalent bonding, and electrostatic interaction. At present, platinum-based drugs can be conjugated with inorganic materials (e.g., carbon materials, mesoporous silica nanoparticles and gold nanomaterials) and organic materials (e.g., polymers, dendrimers, and liposomal micelles) via physical encapsulation, chemical covalent bonding, or electrostatic interaction to achieve drug delivery (Kapadne et al., 2024; Kalayil et al., 2024; Stępień et al., 2025; Santos et al., 2024) Despite the promise of nanotechnology, designing ideal delivery platforms for cervical cancer requires overcoming hurdles such as optimizing drug loading capacity, minimizing premature leakage in systemic circulation, and ensuring spatiotemporally controlled release at the tumor site. Nevertheless, the design of platinum-based drug delivery systems still faces the following challenges: high-efficiency drug loading capacity, reliable premature leakage prevention performance, precise lesion-targeting capability, and controllable drug release efficiency.This review provides a comprehensive overview on the development process, the anti-tumor mechanisms, and the mechanisms of drug resistance of platinum-based drugs. It also elaborates on the current clinical application status and optimization strategies of platinum-based metal drugs in the treatment of cervical cancer, aiming to provide references and insights for future translational medicine research on platinum-based drugs. 2Development process and antitumor mechanismGiven the significant role of platinum-based drugs in the treatment of cervical cancer, we summarize the evolutionary process of these drugs from accidental discovery to systematic development and present their anti-tumor mechanisms (Figure 1).FIGURE 1The structural evolution and clinical categorization of major platinum-based agents.Infographic showing three generations of platinum-based chemotherapy drugs: cisplatin as the first generation with global standard use, carboplatin and nedaplatin as second generation drugs for toxicity reduction, and oxaliplatin as the third generation for overcoming drug resistance. Blue and pink arrows below highlight systemic toxicity reduction and overcoming drug resistance through nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neurotoxicity reduction, DNA damage repair pathway blocking, and drug efflux reduction.2.1Cisplatin: discovery and the gold standard for CCRTCisplatin (cis-[PtCl2(NH3)2]) stands as the pioneering heavy metal coordination compound with broad-spectrum antitumor activity. Since its FDA approval in 1978, it has remained the global gold standard for concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) in cervical cancer (Peyrone, 1844; Rosenberg et al., 1969; Mitsunaga et al., 2011).The cytotoxic mechanism of cisplatin involves the formation of DNA cross-links that inhibit transcription and replication. Upon cellular entry via copper transporters (CTR1), the low intracellular chloride environment triggers the substitution of chloride ligands with water molecules, forming electrophilic aqua-complexes (Holzer et al., 2006) (Figure 2). These positively charged species are subsequently attracted to the negatively charged nuclear DNA and interact with the nucleophilic centers of DNA purine bases (specifically the N7 sites of guanine or adenine). The resulting platinum-DNA adducts bend and distort the DNA structure, inhibit transcription, trigger cell apoptosis, and ultimately lead to cell death (Rocha et al., 2018).FIGURE 2The structure and mechanisms of action of cisplatin (Browning et al., 2017).Illustration of the cellular uptake and action of cisplatin, a chemotherapy drug, showing its entry by passive diffusion or via CTR1 transporter, hydrolysis in reduced chloride environment, and binding to DNA leading to apoptosis if not repaired or resistance if repaired.Despite its clinical efficacy, cisplatin is limited by significant systemic toxicities, most notably nephrotoxicity, which affects approximately 30% of patients at standard therapeutic doses (50–75 mg/m2). Additional complications include neurotoxicity, ototoxicity, and myelosuppression, alongside the persistent challenge of intrinsic and acquired resistance (Chen and Chang, 2019).2.2Structural evolution for toxicity reduction: carboplatin and nedaplatinTo mitigate these adverse effects, second-generation analogues with modified leaving groups were developed to enhance patient tolerability. Carboplatin, characterized by the replacement of chloride ligands with a cyclobutene-1,1-dicarboxylate moiety, represents a significant advancement in structural optimization. This modification increases water solubility 16-fold and slows the drug’s activation kinetics, resulting in a substantially reduced incidence of nephrotoxicity…

full_text_excerpt: This review systematically delineates the evolution of first-to third-generation platinum drugs, elucidating their molecular mechanisms of action specifically within the landscape of cervical cancer. By bridging traditional pharmacology with cutting-edge nanotechnology, this review offers strategic insights into achieving precise delivery and controlled release, potentially defining new paradigms for the next-generation of cervical cancer therapeutics. Nevertheless, the design of platinum-based drug delivery systems still faces the following challenges: high-efficiency drug loading capacity, reliable premature leakage prevention performance, precise lesion-targeting capability, and controllable drug release efficiency.This review provides a comprehensive overview on the development process, the anti-tumor mechanisms, and the mechanisms of drug resistance of platinum-based drugs. Cervical cancer remains a predominant malignancy of the female reproductive system and a critical global health challenge. Traditional platinum-based agents such as cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin, are cornerstones in postoperative adjuvant therapy, management of locally advanced cases, and systemic treatment of recurrent/metastatic disease. However, their clinical efficacy is frequently hampered by severe systemic toxicities and the emergence of chemoresistance. To address these bottlenecks, diverse nano-delivery platforms have been engineered to enhance bioavailability and mitigate adverse effects. Furthermore, we critically evaluate the clinical application of these agents and provide a comprehensive synthesis of recent advances in nano-delivery systems, including targeted and stimuli-responsive carriers. 6ConclusionAs a fundamental drug for anti-tumor treatment, platinum-based drugs…
